en: The Preface:
A separate transmission outside the teachings, not relying on words and letters, pointing directly at the human mind to see one’s nature and become a Buddha.

Thus, for nine years he sat facing a wall, alone attuning to the true mechanism; returning to the West with a single shoe, he originally had nothing more to say. As for standing in the snow and severing his arm—
Those of this school all directly participate in the Supreme Vehicle; their single mind is sealed by mutual accord. What need is there to record their words?
Nevertheless, since the Buddha-dharma entered China, there have already been the Forty-two Chapters; even when Master Lu emerged from Dong’ou, he composed wondrous discourses on the sutras.
What need is there that these words be insufficient to record? Qian resides in a remote frontier region where the Buddha-dharma is rare.
I have heard that during the rebellions at the end of the Ming dynasty, Chan practitioners from all quarters fled their lands to beg for alms.

Amidst this turmoil, some continued to wear the robes and carry the bowls of their tradition without falling away from its ancestral style, while others hung up their wooden boards and suspended their mallets to propagate the Dharma teachings on a grand scale.

Consequently, each lineage came to possess its own recorded sayings (*yulu*). Among these, there are not a few instances where a single phrase used to engage disciples or a word spoken reveals the Way; however, because...
He resides far away at the edge of the heavens, unable to broadcast his teachings throughout the Central Plains or throughout the realm. Master Shanyi secretly laments this;

thus, he has not shunned the hardships of travel to traverse various mountains, extensively collecting the recorded sayings (*yulu*) of various masters and compiling them into a volume titled *Huaideng* (The Lamp of Convergence).
He has come to me seeking a preface, desiring to have it carved into printing blocks. I said to him: "I have heard that when one paints..."
One who paints snow cannot depict its purity; one who paints the moon cannot depict its brilliance; one who paints flowers cannot depict their fragrance;
one who paints a spring cannot depict its sound; and one who paints a person cannot depict their inner sentiment.
Language and written characters are inherently insufficient for revealing the Way. Now that you have compiled the words of various masters, will it not be said [of you] that...?
"Is the Way found here? He replied, "Yes, yes; no, no. Formerly, Dao Fu said: "Do not cling to words and letters, yet do not depart from words and letters;

this is the functioning of the Way. Although the expressions of the various schools today differ in their degree of excellence and their practitioners vary in the depth of their realization, they all belong to the lineage of the School of the Gate and serve to manifest our Way.
Therefore, I wish to entrust this to a famous mountain and disseminate it throughout eminent monasteries. Those with discerning eyes will naturally be able to evaluate it;
I hope that it will not lead others to claim that the frontier regions of the dark lands have not yet heard the Buddha-dharma. This, indeed, is my aspiration. I said:
There is indeed such a thing! It does not reside in language, yet it is not outside of language; one does not cling to written characters, yet one does not depart from them.
This is truly the "separate transmission outside the teachings. Thus, I have appended these remarks at the beginning of the preface.
Written by the mountain man Cheng Chunxiang of Zichi Ji on the day of Jiaping month in the Renwu year of the Kangxi era,
at the Oushi Studio on Beilong.
The Buddha-dharma and the sacred teachings are non-dual. The sacred teachings have overflowed throughout China, extending to the furthest reaches where the sun, moon, frost, and dew reach;
there is nowhere that the teaching of the Sage does not exist. How magnificent! The Buddha-dharma has spread everywhere.

In all places, throughout worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there is nowhere that does not equally receive the moisture of transformation; from the very beginning, there has never been a distinction between this being abundant and that being meager.
Yet, when there are differences in whether [the teaching] is hidden or manifest, these must necessarily await the arrival of the proper time.
When the time has not yet arrived, one cannot force it to proceed; when the time has arrived, one cannot stop it even if one tries. Thus, it revolves between the arrival and non-arrival of the time.

This, then, depends entirely upon the emergence of a heroic and eminent figure who shall shoulder this Way, exhausting their mental faculties and enduring toil and fatigue, accumulating merit over years and months to bring it to completion;
truly, it is not easy to speak of such a thing. Formerly, when the Master edited the *Shi*, he did not include the "Feng" (Air) of Chu;

commentators have taken this to mean that Confucius held it in contempt, yet they failed to realize that at that time, the rites, music, and moral transformation [of that region] were [not yet fully developed].

It flourishes uniquely in the Central Lands; from Jing southward, its songs and ballads have not yet become prominent. Thus, those who collect the customs of the people have had nothing to record there.
Now that the local customs of Chu have ceased, it flourishes among the various Xia states. Qian-nan lies far at the edge of the world, ten thousand *li* from the Central Plains.

Its people’s customs are simple and rustic, and its mountains and rivers are steep and treacherous; the influence of the imperial edicts and teachings hardly reaches it. This is like the case of the "Plucking Flowers" [incident].
As for the single lineage that has continued from the Tang and Song dynasties down to the Ming, it was seldom heard of.
Master Tiantong Shan, filled with compassion, took it upon himself to recover what had been scattered and lost.

He gathered the records of the various masters from the late Ming period down to the present day—those whose conduct surpassed the mundane and whose realization was true—including the *yulu* (recorded sayings) of the fourfold assembly, totaling [such-and-such] volumes.

In ten volumes, these were compiled into a grand collection titled the *Quannan Huizheng Denglu* (The Lamp Record of the Quannan Assembly). Thus, the single lamp of Shaoshi Mountain shines everywhere throughout heaven and earth.
In the summer of the Guiwei year, the printing blocks were sent to the Imperial Library.

Upon passing by me to request a preface, I lamented that the Buddha-dharma in Quannan had been extinguished for several hundred years; I could not have imagined that the time for its resplendent proclamation would arrive on this very day. May it...
Had there not been those with great power and a mind free from suffering, such as the devas and nāgas, then this [teaching] would have ultimately remained unmanifest.

Whether near, among those of the various quarters, or far away, among later students, who would have known that from the ancestors there was this one lineage of the essential Dharma of the patriarchs?

Perhaps it is because the radiance of the various elders of the past shall surely appear in the world that, within the constant light of quiescence (*nitya-śānta-prabhāsvara*), they silently manifest through the devas and nāgas to bring it to completion.

A magnificent achievement! Furthermore, Tianlong was one among those who occupied the ancestral seat; using his present body to examine the property of his own prior lives, he naturally attained precision and correctness.
From this point on, the Buddha-dharma of the region south of the Qin Mountains and that of the Central Plains branched out like two horses galloping side by side, each vying for preeminence.
Is his merit not truly great? Since Tianlong had taken the Buddha-dharma as his own responsibility, now, in the East—

The Southern Dharma lineage has fallen into extreme disorder. Just as Confucius composed the *Spring and Autumn Annals*, recording what was to be recorded and excising what was to be excised, so that the rabble of wild and reckless men could not arrogantly insert themselves to confuse the ancestral succession—this work’s merit in sweeping away such chaos exceeds that of the present record by one degree.
For while this [record] serves to manifest the good, that [Annals] served to suppress the evil; both...
This is the principle of the Spring and Autumn Annals. This constitutes the preface.
Dated the Gui month of the year Kaimei of the Kangxi era.

Preface by Du Zhen, Minister of the Ministry of Rites (with two additional ranks), Director of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, and Lecturer at the Imperial Academy, written for the Source of Enlightenment (*Yuanqi*).
I traveled through the southeast, visiting various great monasteries. During the intervals of my summer retreat, I perused the *Transmission of the Lamp* (*Chuanteng lu*) and observed...

The names of the venerable masters of antiquity and the present day are found mostly in the various provinces of Jiang and Zhejiang; yet, regarding Qianzhong, not even a single word or a speck of ink has been seen.
Unable to restrain myself, I closed the volume and sighed, saying: "Sages and worthies are born regardless of their location, and the Buddha-dharma pervades all places.
Why is it that our Qian alone is without [such traces]? Is this person confined by their land? Or is the Buddha-dharma partial?"

Carrying this thought in my heart, I have wandered through the mists and waters for more than ten years. Upon returning to my native village, I often reflect on those who compiled [the records] during the Tang and Song dynasties;

it seems they considered that our local religious traditions in Qian (Guizhou) had not yet reached their conclusion, and that they were fading away without transmission—this, of course, goes without saying.
From the Ming dynasty down to the Qing, the teachings of our Qian [Guizhou] religious tradition have already spread widely;

moreover, the recorded sayings (*yulu*) of each school circulate and are remarkably worthy of study. When compared with those of other provinces, they are no less significant. Why, then, has there been no transmission of them in recent times?
Is it that the sages and worthies truly choose their place of birth? Or is it that the Buddha-dharma is indeed not universal? I—[the author]—...

It is with a sense of poignant longing that I am moved by this. Yet, upon deeply investigating its origins, I find that because the mountains and passes are so remote, official correspondence cannot reach it;
thus, those who wield the brush have had no means to collect these records. Being of dull wit, I nevertheless respectfully pledge my resolve to do so.
Undaunted by cold or heat, he personally traveled through various prefectures to collect the recorded sayings (*yulu*) of all the masters throughout the entire region of Qian.
Supplementing these with his own limited insights, he compiled them into a work titled *The Record of the Convergence of Lamps in Southern Qian* (*Qian'nan Huīdēnglù*).

He humbly seeks correction from those with clear vision, intending to have it carved into printing blocks and entered into the canon, so that when future individuals of lofty brilliance, far-reaching understanding, impartial mind, and universal virtue appear, they may further refine and compile it for the benefit of future seekers.
May these [fragments] be preserved for a moment; it is my hope that future generations who peruse them will find no cause for regret.

Regarding the general principles of this work, it is appropriate to compile the various provinces together and arrange both ancient and modern materials side by side, so that readers may understand that their origins follow a systematic order.
I have merely examined the records of the various patriarchs throughout successive dynasties preserved within the Tripitaka; these are so numerous as to "drench the oxen and fill the rafters.
Since they have already been widely disseminated, I shall not elaborate further. Moreover, my learning is meager and my wisdom shallow, my knowledge scant and my strength feeble;
I fear only that I might incur the reproach of one who attempts to irrigate the mountains and nourish the sea with a mere drop.

This collection was originally compiled for Qian-nan. Having passed through several instances of warfare and destruction, I feared that the records of the former masters might be lost and fail to reach posterity;
therefore, I have specially gathered them together and deposited them here to bequeath to future students.
The works collected herein are exclusively in the Qian dialect; how could I dare hope to supplement the Dharma-gate?

It is merely that by means of these, I wish to demonstrate that the virtuous people of Qian harmonize with those of all provinces, such that all may be called Buddha-lands, thereby showing that the True Dharma flows everywhere throughout the Eastern Land without interruption.

Regarding the format for compilation: according to ancient precedent, only materials such as formal sermons (*shàngtáng*), informal discourses (*xiǎocān*), instructions to the assembly (*shìzhòng*), recorded encounters (*jīyuán*), verses on cases (*niànsòng*), and dharma talks (*fǎyǔ*) were included;
miscellaneous writings and those with no specific title were not recorded. However, because the region of Qian is remote and sparsely populated, it was impossible to follow this precedent.
Consequently, all that falls within the scope of diligent practice and effort—whether or not it has been formally recorded—is included in the category of miscellaneous writings without exception.
I have collected them all together so that their names may be preserved for future reference; it is not out of a desire to indulge my own inclinations with superfluous additions.

Among the various masters, there were also those who traveled while renting lodgings to propagate the Dharma; I have included only those whose records are extant in the *Qin* (southern) dialect, and I do not dare to record the rest in full detail.
Regarding the schools of our tradition, although it is said there are five houses, in recent times only the Dong and Ji lineages have been practiced in the world.
In the region of Qian, those of the Ji lineage predominate, while there are only a few remaining of the Dong lineage; the origins of both are annotated at the beginning of this volume.
Examining the spiritual tradition of my own lineage in Qian, its flourishing began at the end of the Ming dynasty.
It was from the time that the three masters—Yanju Laoren, Yusheng, and Yunfu Heshang—entered Qian that they broke new ground.

Master Yan’s name begins with the character "Xing" (行), which is why this book first starts with the character "Xing" and concludes with the character "Shi" (實); the remainder shall await future installments.
From the Ming dynasty through to the Qing, there were various masters who propagated the Way in Qian; their recorded sayings (*yulu*) have also been previously carved and included in the canon.
Now, these have again been collected and collated, so that readers may view them in their entirety upon opening the volume, without needing to seek them out elsewhere.
Compiled by Xian An Tianlong, as requested by Chun.
Respectfully recorded at the beginning of the *Catalogue of the Lamp Records of the Quannan Assembly*.

Record of the Lamp of the Southern Circuit of Qianzhou, Volume One.
Compiled by Ruchun of Tianlong at Xian’an,
the thirty-second generation descendant of Linji in the Tian Tong line.
Chan Master Xiangya Ting of Xichan Monastery in Wuchuan was a dharma successor of Chan Master Poshan Ming.
He was the son of the Chen family of Fuzhou. One day, while visiting Wushan Temple, he happened to read the *Chanzong Zhengmai* (The True Lineage of the Chan School).
Upon reaching the passage where an ancient worthy ascended the hall and held up his staff, saying: "The Dharma-body is formless," yet...

While currently manifesting his form here, he stirred himself from worldly thoughts. He paid homage to the Venerable Changxi Fu when the latter shaved his head and personally attended the lectures of Dharma Master Kerong, yet he did not find their teachings to his satisfaction.
Upon arriving at Huangbo, he met Master Zhong, who instructed him to investigate the "Mu" (無) koan.
After three years without realization, he went to Gushan to attend upon Master Wuyi, where he changed his practice to investigate "All dharmas return to One. He then returned to Huangbo.
He visited Master Mi (Miyun Yuanwu) and found that his initial awakening (*shijue*) was truly effective. Consequently, he received full ordination under the Master and subsequently left Fujian.

He traveled to Jinsu Temple, but after a long time, the karmic conditions did not harmonize there. Later, he visited Master Poshan and received formal certification (*inko*). Upon ascending the hall, he said:

"When the Dharma-vehicle is proclaimed, the souls of those on the Ten Stages tremble; when the True Eye is opened, the hearts of those on the Three Grades of Sainthood quiver. Even if a hair were to swallow the vast ocean, and a mustard seed..."
To bring Mount Sumeru here would already be falling behind. But as for the phrase that points upward—how is it?
He held up his staff and said: "From this point on, one need not go; upon returning, one attains it. Who can vie with the misty scenery of the Five Lakes? He ascended the hall and said:
"Kāśyapa saw the World-Honored One hold up the flower, and in accordance with the occasion, he broke into a smile. Subhūti saw the World-Honored One..."

Discussing the sutras and explaining their essential meanings, they wept and wailed with grief. O Great Assembly, when these two great masters—one laughing and one weeping—they could not avoid each seeing only one side.
I, this mountain monk, shall specifically provide a verse for them: Sometimes laughing, sometimes weeping, The seven stars cast oblique reflections as he sweeps away the demon’s lair.
A single arrow brings down twin eagles in the azure void; Six times six remains, still thirty-six. (He strikes the meditation staff.)
"Ha! Entering the hall: Standing like a cliff ten thousand fathoms high, it is difficult to find a foothold; those with copper heads and iron jaws labor in vain with their conjectures.
The peach blossoms red and the pear blossoms white are truly Maitreya; laughing, he points south toward Nanquan, where Sudhana dwells. Does the assembly see Sudhana?"

[The Master] leaned on his staff, gave a shout, and descended from the seat. He ascended the hall and said: "The mountain colors are as dense as dark eyebrows; the oriole’s song is about to flow forth.

This clearly proclaims the intent of the Patriarchs—what need is there to seek elsewhere? If you can realize it in this way, then everyone possesses the original source that encompasses all phenomena;
every individual is the wondrous essence that fills the ten directions. But tell me: where do the mountains, rivers, and the great earth reside?"
He remained seated for a long while, then said, "Enter [the Hall]. He ascended the hall and said: "Before the fifteenth day, the person of no rank shoulders snow to fill the well.
After the fifteenth day, the person of no rank holds a conch-shell ladle to measure the sea. On the very fifteenth day itself—"
Now tell me: what livelihood does the "True Person of No Station" have? He plucks the vermilion cassia from the moon amidst the clouds; he gathers the jade flowers from heaven while the rain falls.
[He] strikes the meditation seat and descends. On the occasion of the New Year, he ascends the hall: "The first day of the new year begins the reign; all things are renewed.
The precious mirror hangs high, and the myriad phenomena present their splendor. May the imperial wind forever fan, and may the Buddha-sun shine long."
When the qilin appears, the halberds and spears are laid to rest; when the phoenix emerges, civil virtue is cultivated.

The patch-robed monks of the four seas blow the new dharma-conch and beat the new dharma-drum; they wield the new staff and expound the new dharma-meanings, together offering prayers for peace and prosperity.
But prior to the undifferentiation of the single breath, how was it? "A few sounds of the clear chime are beyond right and wrong; there is but one idle man."
Between heaven and earth, he ascended the hall. A monk asked, "I do not ask about ascending the hall for the sake of the assembly; how is it before you have even left the abbot’s quarters?
The Master said, "The sun and moon do not move, yet the universe is dark. He then continued: "The entirety of empty space is a single ancient mirror.
Within it are ten billion fragrant seas, ten billion Mount Sumerus, the great earth, mountains, rivers, grasses, trees, and forests."
Whether saint or ordinary person, monastic or layperson, man or woman, noble or lowly, sentient or insentient—all are contained within this.
Why then is not even a shadow of the water-buffalo of Mount Mui to be seen? After a long silence, he said:
"Sleeping on one's head and lying on one's back, no one recognizes it; ten thousand miles of blue sky, a single hook of the moon. He ascended the hall and said: "Five times five is twenty."
Five. Opening the treasury of jewels, scattering priceless treasures as offerings to countless Buddhas—tell me now, who is the one making the offering?
Who is the one receiving it? *Thut!* It brings to mind Xie Sanlang, rowing his oars by himself beneath the moon.

Ascending the hall to mark the conclusion of the retreat: to speak of mind and nature is like entering the sea to count the sands; to cite the ancients and the present is like grasping at the moon in the waves.
Deshan used the staff and Linji used the shout—though their intentions were good, in the end they were great errors.
But tell me, as Xichan concludes the retreat today, how will you instruct us? Striking the meditation seat, he said: "When meeting a person who has attained the Way on the road..."
"Do not respond with speech or silence. [The Master] ascends the hall and says: "Throughout the day, all is manifest and majestic; no one understands how to bring it forth.
It tires that Wood Seat Monk to prattle on and engage in mistaken deliberation. He holds up his staff and says: "Now, as for what this Wood Seat Monk deliberates upon—what principle is it?
If you say there is a principle, 'existence' is itself emptiness. If you say it is the principle of emptiness, 'emptiness' is itself existence. If..."
If you say the Way is neither existent nor empty, that is a coarse and superficial Buddha-nature. If you say the Way is both existent and empty, that is a clumsy and unrefined True Suchness.
Since these four meanings are all incorrect, tell me, O Great Assembly: what meaning is it that you are deliberating upon?

Holding up his staff, he drew a circle (○) and said: "The pines and cypresses stand unevenly as thin smoke gathers; the layered peaks and ridges are slow to receive the rising moon. He ascended the hall and said:
"On the eighth day of the fourth month every year, the fragrant water bathes Siddhārtha. To whom does the handle of the ladle point? One mouth drinks from a thousand rivers.
If you can understand this, then in every dust mote and every world-system [is the truth]. If you do not understand, I shall give you a kick right over the head. He stood upright.
Holding up his staff, he said, "Śākyamuni the Old Man has arrived. Do you all see him? He struck the staff and said, "Zha! Ascending the hall, he said:
"The sound of the stream rings; the bright moon descends. Heyshan beats the drum; Puhua shakes the bell.
The five ranks and three mysteries, the nine bands and four impossibilities—such worn-out vines of entanglement as these have no use here at all. You all..."
"O people, how will you search for it? In the end, the frosty night moon falls spontaneously into the stream before you.
He then offered a verse on the story of Peak Master’s pillow, saying: "Eagerly gazing at the bright moon, I wandered alone; I entered the reeds and did not return."
By the side of the white stone pillow, a dream is startled into breaking; the wind blows open the bamboo gate of the ancient temple. As for Deshan’s staff—one blow leaves a trace;
a thousand mountains are all split asunder. Alas, the toothless barbarian! He did not know the secret of settling the mind. Bodhidharma faced the wall;
for nine years he faced the wall until his tongue grew hair. He deceived Shen Guang into taking a single stroke of the blade—already it was too late.
The wind and waves arose of their own accord; even now, the billows surge across the level plains.

Chan Master Yueshi Luan’s Dharma heir, Chan Master Yusong Chuanxi of West Mountain in Guiyang, was the son of the Song family from Western Sichuan. Having lost both parents in his youth, he was raised by his grandmother.
When he reached the age of twenty-three, his grandmother passed away. Thereupon, at the White Crane Hermitage in his native district, he paid homage to Master Xingkong.
The Elder left the household life and cultivated the practice of patience. One day, following the guidance of a traveling monk, he went to visit Master Poxue, where he attained realization.
After receiving full ordination, he served the master diligently for six years; whenever he posed difficult questions or engaged in debate, his fellow practitioners were all moved to admiration.

Upon the passing of Poxue, the Master resolved to travel widely to seek instruction. Arriving in Chongqing, he met with Master Changpo Gao, who provided him with certification of his realization. Later, he entered Qian Province and established the Dharma at Mou.
He established Nishan Baoguo Chan Temple and further opened Xishan Chuanfa Temple. Later, he resided at Dingshan Qianming Temple in Dingzhou.
Retiring from his post, he traveled through Jiangsu and Zhejiang, ascending to Tiantong to pay respects at the stupa of Master Mi. Due to illness, he passed away while seated;
his disciples escorted his remains back to Qian, where they built a stupa beside the Phoenix Pond on the western mountain. [Upon entering the hall for the formal discourse,] he was asked:

"Master, how do you understand this? The Master said, "He is the lord of the myriad phenomena; he does not wither with the four seasons. Yaoming then commanded him to compose a verse.
The Master spontaneously recited: "The old man Zhaozhou is truly reckless; He points out the cypress tree before the hall for one to see.

It is only because people fail to realize its clarity That so many throughout ancient and modern times have suffered in their delusion. Yaoming again commanded him to compose a verse on the story of drinking tea.
The Master composed a verse, saying: "How laughable is Old Zhaozhou, the master craftsman! He dug a pit on level ground to test dragons and snakes.
Whenever they met, he would simply say, 'Go drink tea. How many have ever known that the road was not far? Yaya caused the Master to remain and receive full ordination.
Later, Yaya tested him again with the story of Zhaozhou visiting two hermit masters. The Master once more gave the same answer as Wuyi. One day, the Master took his leave of Yaya. Furthermore...
Jinmin met Shu. Upon seeing the Master arrive, Shu immediately asked, "You have been away from this old monk for several years;
where have you been all this time? The Master replied, "The province of Qian. Shu said, "Regarding the seasonal goods of Qian, are prices high or low these days?
The Master said, "When the Abbot arrives there, you will naturally know. Shu said, "If that is so, then you have missed the mark. The Master said, [I have not].
"Today you have come again and run into this fellow," Baizhang said. "I would give you thirty blows of the staff; tell me, was that a reward or a punishment?
The Master replied, "There is an eye upon the tip of the staff. One day, Baizhang tested him again with the story of Lingyun’s awakening upon seeing peach blossoms;
the Master answered without hesitation. Baizhang then wrote out the lineage transmission and entrusted it to him. He ascended the hall and said: "At the summit of Mount Yuntai..."
Standing apart from the mundane world, he upheld the ultimate core of the monks and revealed the profound and essential mechanisms of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
Looking left and right, he said: "At such a moment as this, one severs all worldly stimuli within the palm of one's hand and hangs the precious sword upon the brow.
The Buddhas of the three periods are rendered speechless and tongue-tied; the Patriarchs of the six generations suppress their breath and swallow their voices. Their merit is supreme."
A thousand ages. Standing like a cliff ten thousand fathoms high. When the true command is exercised, the ten directions are cut off at once.
Reaching this point, one truly knows that there is a path leading upward. "Great assembly, do you know the path leading upward? After a long silence, he said:

"The front peak rises high beyond the cry of the solitary wild goose; with no one to take my hand, with whom can I walk? He gave a shout and descended from his seat. [Ascending the hall: "The patched robe..."
The nostrils of the Sangha; the heart-mind and essence of the Patriarchs and Buddhas. Whether you understand or do not understand, it is all contained therein.
But tell me, what is within? He then struck the ground with his staff and said: "This very staff points south of Annam and blocks north of Beipiao; it indicates the west and carves the east."
"Having arrived here, you may at will capture tigers and rhinoceroses alive, or seize fierce dragons in their raw state.
Even if Mañjuśrī or Samantabhadra were to arrive, they would have to surrender with hands bound. Śākyamuni and Maitreya would find themselves compelled to withdraw;

let alone those of the Three Grades of Sages losing heart, even those of the Ten Stages would be struck with terror. Were it not for the right person, it would be difficult to fully comprehend this. He ascended the hall and said: "The thousand sages..."
Transcending the world, one must investigate the single mind alone. The teachings established by the Five Houses are a direct pointing and a single transmission;

the Three Vehicles and the twelve divisions of the scriptures are all but redundant words, and the seventeen hundred cases are entirely idle talk. Those who rely on words and linger in phrases bury their own family treasure;
those who grasp at staffs and doubt shouts have not yet penetrated the source. To speak thus, even if it were to moisten the lips and touch the teeth—nevertheless...
This is already groundless. *Duḥ!* Zen Master Zhonghe Tianhu Zhengyin of Sinnan was the son of the Li family from Chongqing in Shu.

He studied under Venerable Minshu, thoroughly realized the source and bottom, and personally received his seal of approval. He ascended the hall and said: "When the lion roars, the fragrant grasses are green."
The patch-robed monks of the world cannot leap out; where the Elephant King walks, the tracks of foxes vanish. Those with iron brows and copper heads have their bones shattered by the blow;
Daowei’s staff sends Xiangyan off. Before Yangshan’s hall, the round mirror shatters. The poisonous vapor wafts forth, ever-new through the ages;
this is the true face of every person, most intimate. Originally there is not a single dharma to give to anyone—this shall surely bring peace to a thousand feet.

[He] gave [it] to the Ten-Thousand-Footed One. *Du!* On the eighth day of the twelfth month, he ascended the hall. Having abandoned the imperial palace for the Snow Mountains, he lived amidst knee-deep reeds and wild grasses.
Unaware that six years had turned into a calamity, the morning star shattered his eyes into emptiness.
Looking left and right, he said: "Do you see Old Śākyamuni? Without passing through kalpas, one attains the Dharmakāya; the nostrils remain as they were before."

Lips meet. Entering the hall. Closing the door to sit in meditation. Receiving those of the highest capacity. Looking into the mirror and wincing; bending down to accommodate those of middling and lower capacities.
Looking at the assembly, he held up his whisk and asked, "Do you see? He struck the meditation seat and asked, "Do you hear?
He gave a shout and said, "When a character is transcribed three times, 'wu' becomes 'an' and 'an' becomes 'ma'. Entering the hall: "If you go this way, the Second Patriarch bowed and returned."

The old position: coming thus. When the Pine-Planting Master came forth from Huangmei, it was "in the midst of non-suchness, yet suchness. Three times he struck the staff, yet there was no connection.
"In the midst of suchness, yet not suchness": the red-bearded man bumps into the red-bearded barbarian.

[He] ascended the hall: "The primary meaning is bright and vivid; one does not cling to the two extremes, nor is the Middle Way established. One's body manifests throughout the entire world like the moon."
Facing the autumn blue. When Śākyamuni saw the morning star, the calamity reached his descendants and has lasted until this day.
Consider the Dharma Hall discourse of Chan Master Dongshan Yingxiu of Nan’an Huacheng: “Leaving behind appearances to manifest the center; within it, the excellence is unfathomable.
Truly, when things are understood, the ultimate truth remains unmoved by activity or stillness. Therefore it is said: ‘It is like empty space.’”

The substance relies upon the various phenomena to manifest its brilliance. Even in all speech, silence, words, and deeds, the thousand differences are unified by a single thread, and the myriad varieties share one mind.
It simply requires every person to reflect inwardly and turn the light back upon themselves, investigating the ultimate abode of their own original life-spirit.
When active, it is like drifting clouds and flowing water; when still, the mind opens up in radiant clarity. Furthermore—

"A single phrase: neither moving nor still. How do you speak of this? "The crane has nine gao of space, yet its wings find it hard to soar; the horse lacks a thousand li, so its pursuit of the wind is in vain.
With a shout, he descended from his seat. Ascending the hall, he said: "The Great Way penetrates the heavens; its majestic light encompasses the earth."

Fundamentally, one shares the same root as the Buddhas and Patriarchs; humans and devas are of one substance. Within the three thousandfold world system, there is nothing that does not receive this pivotal mechanism;
beneath the entire heavens, there is none who does not rely upon this power of grace. It gathers and encompasses all in perfect fusion, its application being boundless.
Even if a thousand sages or ten thousand sages were to appear, they could not shift it by so much as a single hair’s breadth—just as was the case with Linji, Deshan, and Shishuang.

Yunmen: Each manifests the extraordinary; it can cover both sound and form, spanning from antiquity to the present, rivaling the sages and transcending the worthies, gloriously illuminating the sun of the Buddha.
It does not go beyond this very thing. Great assembly, if you proceed in this manner, it is like the wind blowing and the grass bowing;

if you do not proceed in this manner, it is like the grass bowing and the wind blowing. But as for that single phrase which does not move its sharp edge—how will you speak? (He remained silent for a long while.)
He said: "At the tip of the staff, the True Eye opens; from the Dharma-realm, the Heart-Jewel is spat forth. He ascended the hall and said:
"It is not the mind, it is not the Buddha—this is still like driving a stake into empty space. To act thus is not permitted; not to act thus is also not permitted.
Why trouble to dig up the earth to search for the heavens? Great assembly, you must know this news: right here, cut off all manifold differences. Not...
Separated by not even a hair’s breadth. To receive it directly in one's very being is to stand like a wall ten thousand fathoms high. Do you understand this yet? After a long silence, he said:
"Before the empty kalpa, all sons of the Buddha—the head-word is never raised, yet it is naturally square and round."
Master Hui of Tiantong ascended the hall at Anshun Changshou Temple and addressed the assembly: "That which cannot be depicted is a single segment of celestial mechanism, revealed day after day.

That which cannot be painted is a point of profound mystery, proclaimed moment by moment. Continuous and unceasing, the creative power of the Great Transformation and the Mother of Transformation weave together an ancient brocade.
Dense and intricate, names and titles are manifested, fashioned into golden gauze. I, this mountain monk, now..."

On this day, facing the seat of the King of Jewel Flowers, I have brought it forth directly before you. I desire only that each and every person take full responsibility for it and accept it in its entirety.
Should you hesitate or deliberate, I shall further break through the matter for you all. [He] threw down his staff, clapped his hands, laughed "he-he," and descended from the seat.
Entering the hall, he said: "The Way is vast, profound, and perfect; it transcends emotion and leaves behind views. When encountering objects, it responds. When meeting...
The conditions are immediately manifest; they pervade everywhere and are clearly evident in every place. When wearing clothes and eating meals, do not deviate from the ordinary.

Thoroughly penetrating both action and withdrawal, one does not move a single step. Majestic, towering, and profoundly still, steadfastly radiating brilliance, one stands preeminent and transcends the crowd, fundamentally free from all fetters and attachments.
Whether turning or pausing, bowing or rising, letting go or gathering in—tell me, is it thus or is it not? Look!

Examine their brows and eyes. How far apart are they? Making a gesture with his hand as if propping up his eyebrows, he said: "The two pupils are clear and piercing, possessing a thousand kinds of artistry;
yet it is difficult to equal the venerable one whose brow arches upward. Entering the hall, he said: "Every house has its door; every household has its path.
Yet within, there is one person whose body has no going, staying, entering, or exiting. In ordinary speech and movement, there is also the acting of a servant."

Master, there are those who hold power and those who receive emoluments. If you say that he knows because he encounters conditions and meets circumstances, striking against them wherever he goes, then why does he lose his nostrils everywhere?
Tell me, is it that which knows, or is it that which does not know? Try to speak on this!
On the Buddha’s Day of Enlightenment, Chan Master Xiangshan Shengfu of Jiangkou ascended the hall and said: "Today is the eighth day of the twelfth lunar month; Śākyamuni attained full realization.
Suddenly beholding the morning star, he gouged out both his own eyes until they were blind. Old Gautama! What a wretched fellow!
He should be pushed right out through the triple gates, left to be tossed by the wind and rained upon as he pleases. Even so, it is not yet finished."
I have not failed him. For forty-nine years he preached the Dharma—speaking of the Dharma as neither Dharma nor non-Dharma—and left five thousand and forty-eight disciples in disarray.
When examined closely, it makes one laugh until one collapses at the Twelve Gorges of Wushan.

(He lets out a shout: "Just so! On the New Year’s Day, he ascended the hall. Times are clear and the land is peaceful; all things flourish and the myriad sounds arise. Rain and wind are harmoniously regulated throughout the eight directions.

Ascending the hall, he said: "This morning is the Mid-Autumn Festival. The vast sky holds a bright, clear moon; ten thousand miles away, not a speck of cloud remains.

Do you understand? When Lord Zhang drinks, Lord Li gets drunk; after they have drunk their fill, they return home side by side, their bridles held across one another.

Yunmen laughed himself to death, wishing to strike them down. [The Master] suddenly picks up his staff, strikes it once, and says:

[He] gave a shout and said: "The Linji school is revived; the unconditioned transformation is upheld.
Having swept the stupa of Master Jiefan Xing, auspicious qi arises at the edge of the *prātimokṣa*. Its light swallows the Buddha-sun and steams the heavens and earth.

Now, by sweeping and paying respects, I repay this profound kindness. At the head of the dry dung-stick, all is vividly clear. [He] inserted incense and said: "The precept-moon is solitary and full, beyond concealment."
The treasury of true fragrance penetrates directly to my master’s nostrils. On the anniversary of the Buddha’s birth, he ascends the hall;

he does not tread the paths of ordinary beings or sages, nor does he dwell within the den of birth and death. He alone reveals the eternal and unchanging, without maintaining any reflected image. With his body stretched across the heavens beyond, he strides alone through the great square.
Thus, when the Elder Śākyamuni first emerged from his mother’s womb, he pointed one finger toward heaven and one finger toward earth.
He walked seven steps in every direction and looked around the four quarters, saying, "In all the heavens above and the earth below, I alone am honored.
Later, Yunmen said, "If I had seen him then, I would have struck him dead with a single blow and fed him to the dogs, just to ensure peace throughout the world.
Looking at it today, these two seem very much like one person supporting the head and another supporting the tail—mutually obstructing one another.
These words of this mountain monk contain two points of defeat. If those in robes and the laity can grasp them, then the old woman was originally but a young bride.
If this is not yet so, then it remains as before: striking the third watch at midday. On the Buddha’s Birthday, I ascend the hall:
the spark struck from flint, the flash of lightning. To hesitate is to be worlds apart; to blink is to fall into a pit. This is no coarse speech.
To deceive people! For now, I have cut off all paths. Here and now, this mountain monk brandishes the sword of killing and giving life; he wields the mechanism of a flashing lightning bolt.
One by one, he unties adhesions and removes bonds, pulls out wedges and extracts nails, so that everyone may attain immediate and thorough penetration, never again to sink into birth and death.
Each one shall be like the Elder Śākyamuni, honored everywhere. Do you see the World-Honored One?
There is none. After a long silence, he struck the ground once with his staff, gave a shout, and descended from the seat.
He addressed the assembly: “The conduct of a practitioner lies in the ordinary. Raise your eyebrows and do not let it pass. With a lofty and dignified nose, there is nothing complex;

throughout the entire body, one is elegant and lively. At the critical juncture of contact and avoidance, everything is shattered through and through. Why must one laboriously force a breakthrough by looking outward?”
When empty space is pulverized, who would know? Walk, stand, sit, or lie down as you please. [The Master] picks up his whisk and sweeps once, saying: "Does the assembly see?
This white whisk in my hands—should even the Buddhas and Patriarchs come, I will not let them pass.
Why is this so? It is simply that letting them pass is not permissible. On New Year's Day, he addressed the assembly: "The Buddha-sun shines forth once more."
The Patriarchal Way is renewed; the rare flower first claims the spring of the Upper Garden. When the human mind is free of concerns, the clay ox bellows;

when the celestial movement is harmonious, the stone tiger stretches. Sweeping away the wind and banner, he transcends antiquity; with staff in hand, he eliminates mountains and waters, severing all ties of intimacy.
Now, all are bathed in the Imperial transformation; throughout the land, they enjoy its grace and look up to supreme benevolence. Yunmen raised [the case] because a monk asked: "One..."
"If a thought does not arise, is there still any fault? The Master said, "The story of Mount Sumeru. The verse says: "A single thought does not arise;
A thousand differences, ten thousand errors. Atop the summit of Mount Sumeru, Neither being nor non-being is clung to. Take care, you followers of Chan!

This intimate phrase— Do not needlessly seek bonds for yourself where none exist. [This concludes] the verse on Zhaozhou visiting the two hermits: Entering the tiger's den to search for the tiger’s cub.
Releasing both and gathering both, exhausting all clever devices; Zhaozhou’s application was originally no different. Though many recognize it, those who truly understand it are rare.
Master Xingtú of Huaguang Temple in Guizhou ascends the hall: "The moon reflects in the cold pond; autumn waters share the vastness of the sky."
A single color: the mountain mists cloak the purple peaks; the setting glow flies side by side with the solitary wild goose. The scenery remains as it was, yet not a single point can be overlooked.
Where the dust of emotion finds its place, how dare the six gates deceive themselves? (He plants his staff and descends from the seat.)

Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "When the sky is clear, the earth is dry; when it rains, the road is wet. All this is the mechanism of the present moment, and it is not something external to the mind.
Alas! Those who head toward the Way waste their efforts halfway through; they are not as good as the old farmer whose entire being is devoid of breath.
Yet where there is breath—mountains in Qian, waters in Chu—the four seas and five lakes are all within the realm of the King’s transformation. When lost..."
Wearing a straw hat, I have traversed a thousand mountains. At the moment of awakening, returning home is simply being oneself.

*Tu!* [He] ascended the hall and said: "In Zen, one studies to see one's nature; in the Way, one studies to clarify the mind. Moment by moment, return to the ultimate reality; at all times, do not seek it elsewhere.
Smash through the cave of ignorance and overturn the tangled vines of delusion. Only when you reach the ground of non-doubt will you finally behold the family treasure. But tell me: after seeing it,"
"How is it? After a long silence, he said: "When hungry, eat; when cold, wear clothes; sit in meditation when at leisure; sleep when weary.
Master Jingkongming of Bianqiao Yuntai gave this discourse on the hall. As Master Panshan said: "The moon of the mind is solitary and full."
Light swallows the myriad phenomena; light does not illuminate the object, nor does the object exist. When both light and object are forgotten, what is it? Dongshan said:
"When light and object have not yet been forgotten, what is it? Elder Dahui said: "A white egret descends to the field—a thousand dots of snow;
a yellow oriole perches on a tree—a single branch of blossoms. Observe these three great elders as they respond to the moment and bring forth [the truth] in accordance with the season.
I hold to this one matter: it is essential that people not be turned by sounds, forms, objects, or external things. At this very moment, turn the light back upon itself and reflect;

recognize the source. Today, I, this old monk, likewise bring it up for you in this way, also desiring that you all, at this very moment, turn the light back upon yourselves and recognize the source of your own selves. Do you recognize it? After a long silence, he said: "Wrong."
Ascending the hall, [the Master] raised the example of Zen Master Zhenjing’s address to the assembly, which said: "Heaven and earth share the same root as I;
the myriad things are one body with me. From head to tail, they are arranged horizontally and vertically. When a fire breaks out on Mount Lu in the north, it burns the eyebrows of Śakra.
The Dragon King of the Eastern Sea cannot endure the pain and lets out a single crash of thunder, which causes the mountain torrents to overflow and the seas to overturn."
Yue: The clouds darken the vast sky. At the crossroads, Old Man Liao, startled awake from his drunkenness, rises and slaps his palms together, laughing loudly:
"In the city of Yunchang, there have lately been few thieves. He then picks up his staff and says: "Thieves! Thieves!"
The Master said: "At that time, when Old Man Zhenjing made such a proclamation, he was much like one whose eyes looked down upon the four seas with no one beside him.
It is a pity that the assembly missed the opportunity at Yuntai; had they been of this caliber on that day, they would have rightly returned his challenge with a 'Duh!
right to his face. Look at his skin—where would it have been placed?"
Chan Master Lingchan Chisong of Guiyang Qianling was the son of the Han family of Tongchuan in Shu. His mother was surnamed Xie.

Because of the chaos of the times, he entered Qian. At the age of fifteen, he took delight in transcending the mundane world and subsequently entered Nanwang Mountain, where he lived in seclusion for several years.
He traveled to Jiufeng to attend upon Master Lingyao. Lingyao instructed him to investigate the koan, "The myriad dharmas return to one. Later, he received the tonsure at the feet of Baiyun Xishi.

He studied under Master Minshu, through whom he attained enlightenment and received formal certification. He remained in seclusion for three years, after which he emerged to establish the Dharma at Qianling.
For over thirty years, he traveled to transform others, and his Way flourished throughout the region of Qian. Monastics from across the lakes and seas heard of him...

The wind gathered in a swirl beneath his seat; more than several dozen people attained the Dharma. He compiled five volumes [of his teachings], which have already been carved and included in the Great Canon (*Dazang*).
Since the Master’s lifelong vow was to remain at Qianling, his disciples built a stupa for him in advance on the southern slope of the mountain.
As he ascended the hall, staff and alms bowl followed him. "The white clouds filling the valley cannot detain him; straw sandals upon his feet follow along."
Along the path, fragrant grasses carpet the way as one approaches. At every step, one treads upon solid ground; at every stage, one penetrates the profound source.

Reaching this point, I cannot bear to spare my own awkwardness and must bring forth before the assembly that "meaningless matter" entrusted to me by that faceless old man whom I encountered long ago. Now tell me: what is this "meaningless matter"?

[The Master] spoke on the matter of flavor. After a long silence, he threw down his whisk and descended from the seat. He ascended the hall and said: "Snow accumulates upon the ten thousand mountains like jade;

the passes and rivers for ten thousand *li* are pure. The light of the mind is beyond compare; it topples the wall of precepts and proceeds. Why is this? The phenomena are of one family; the source of principle is non-dual.
One attains the untainted study, complete with morality, concentration, and wisdom. Do you still recognize the Dharma of the Bodhisattva’s Mind-Ground?"
"Mon! [He] strikes the sounding block once and says, "Listen closely, listen closely. [Ascending the hall: "His descent into the royal palace pointed to heaven and earth;
his manner was too full of careless exposure. It was all because he took seven steps that year, that now everywhere there run about these Zen practitioners.
[Ascending the hall: "If you say 'this very mind is Buddha,' you cannot avoid adding a tip to an arrowhead. If you say 'it is not...'"
"The mind is not the Buddha. This too is merely raising the voice to stop the echo; to bring up one thing is to fail to bring up two. To let this one point pass is to fall into the present moment.
Ten thousand phenomena cannot confine it; a thousand sages cannot pull it back. Ultimately, how would you say it? After a long silence, he said:
"The Wheel-Turning King’s full majesty; the precious seal is naturally sovereign. He ascended the hall. A marvel of a thousand years...

Meeting [the Teacher] in a single morning, one fully transcends once the Great Matter is clearly understood. Although one has stepped upon the path back to the source, when it comes to its profound depths, it is even more desolate and silent.
Therefore it is said: "The Way of the Patriarchs is long and far; only after enduring diligent suffering for a long time can it be perfected."
If you have already attained this realization, lifting your foot you immediately transcend the thousands of sages; within a single hair-tip of the great trichiliocosm, you ascend to the Dharma Hall.
This fundamental vehicle of the school transcends ten thousand functions; not a single speck of dust is established, cutting off all discursive thought.
It is vividly clear and distinct, boundless and limitless. Is it neither Buddha nor mind—who else could it be? Who else could it be? Yet, how wondrous! To recognize it is already not it.
"This is it. This is precisely the phrase where the human realm and the objective world are clearly distinguished; turning one’s body around, one tramples the five Sumeru mountains flat.
Tell me, what kind of person walks this path? After a long silence, he said: "The Heart-Seal of the Patriarchs, the mechanism of the Iron Ox. Ascending the hall:

The first day of the year has just passed, and now comes the Lantern Festival. A bright moon is clearly stamped in the center of the sky. What a fine phrase for the state prior to birth—utterly clear.
It is clearly present before one’s eyes. Above, it is originally and naturally filled with radiance; yet in this world, there are times when the moon is but half-full.
