A monk asked, "The Venerable Piṇḍola heads the offerings of the four worlds daily; does he come here as well?
The Master said, "With what do you intend to make your offering? The monk was speechless. The Master said, "One must not play with the Holy Monk. One day—
A monk came before the barrier and asked, "In the past, when Maitreya snapped his fingers, the gates of the pavilion opened and he bade Sudhana enter.
Today, I have arrived, yet no one snaps their fingers. I wish to enter this pavilion and meet with the Master;
may I do so? The Master said, "Blind! The monk said, "If that is so, then I shall present myself face-to-face. The Master—
[The Master] said, "The Kingdom of Silla is located on the southern edge of the sea. The monk said, "I have arrived here, yet I still do not understand.
The Master then struck him and said, "This old monk has never failed anyone."
Xian Anshishan Yu Xianying Chan Master was the son of the Long family from Fengdu in Shu. His mother was Lady Fan.

Due to the upheavals of the times, he followed his father into military service and entered Qian. Upon reaching Tiantai Mountain in Anping, he paid respects to Master Hengxiu and received the tonsure and full ordination. He followed Master Heng in the founding and development of Shishan.
After Master Heng passed away, the Master succeeded him in guarding the monastery. Vowing to travel as a wandering monk, he received full ordination under the venerable Master Minshu.
Later, he received the seal of approval from Master Tianhou. He subsequently opened a Dharma seat at Fashishan, where he planned to spend his final years.
His disciples had already constructed a stupa at the foot of the mountain for him. Upon ascending the hall, he said: "There is a thing, bright and vivid, yet pitch black.
It is constantly present within all movement and activity, yet it cannot be grasped within that movement and activity. Since it cannot be grasped, tell me: when you eat your rice, where is it?"
Putting on clothes, defecating and urinating, welcoming guests and attending to visitors—what is it that performs these actions and movements?
Today, this mountain monk, not sparing a single hair of his eyebrows, has spread the eight characters wide open for all of you; I have revealed my head and face for you.
Do you all understand this thoroughly? If you do understand it thoroughly, then indeed it is as it naturally is, clearly manifest and vividly apparent.

If you cannot grasp it through exhaustive investigation, return to the old way and leave it as pitch-black. (He lets out a shout and descends from his seat. Entering the hall: In early summer the heat gradually increases;
in mid-winter the cold is severe. When it is hot, heaven and earth are hot throughout; when it is cold, heaven and earth are cold throughout.
If one were to propagate this according to worldly conventions, one would fall into hell like an arrow shot. If one treats this as a matter for deliberation within the Buddha-dharma—
"In what year of the donkey’s life have you even dreamed of this? Ultimately, how should one act? [The Master] strikes the ground with his staff and says:
"Filling the ditches and blocking the ravines—no one understands; after the rain, the autumn waters in the night pond run deep. He ascends the hall and says:

"The Great Way is vast and clear, solitary and vividly manifest. In motion, it extends horizontally throughout the ten voids; in stillness, it is a silver mountain and an iron wall. Therefore it is said: 'If released, then...'"
It fills the six directions; yet when rolled up, it is hidden away in the profound mystery.

Within this, whether wide or narrow, large or small, long or short, square or round—once you have realized there is not even a hair’s breadth of fault or affliction, it is evident that everything naturally accords with what is appropriate.
But how is it that "everything naturally accords with what is appropriate"? Red clouds pierce the azure void; the white sun circles Mount Sumeru. [Thus he ascended the hall.]
Heaven attains the One and becomes clear; Earth attains the One and becomes tranquil; when the sovereign attains the One, all under heaven is at peace;

when the ministers attain the One, they assist the state and bless the people; when the common folk attain the One, they establish their households and sustain their livelihoods; when the patch-robed monks attain the One, the assembly gathers like clouds from the seas.
[The Master] suddenly picks up his staff and says: "Look! Look! This staff has attained the One and directly benefits people. And yet—"
"What is the point of direct penetration? He struck the meditation seat once and said, "One arrow hits the red heart. He addressed the assembly: "Fire moves upward and water flows downward.

When the Patriarchs came from the West, they had no other words. If you do not take these words as the vehicle of our school, the sickness of ten thousand kalpas and a thousand eons will be difficult to extricate.
If you take these words as the vehicle of our school, then within the gate of the patch-robed monks, they are fit only to be put to the test."
[The Master] struck him. Then he said, "Let us consider this: what further excellence is there within the gate of the patch-robed monks? After a long silence, he said:
"When a shadowless tree is planted, no one sees it; yet when its roots are firm, the flowers of wisdom bloom."
Master Hóngxiān Wàndé Yúlín was the son of Zhū of Western Shǔ. His mother was Lù.
Due to the chaos of the times, he entered Qián and took up residence at Yuánzhào Ān on Shuǐqiáo in Ānshùn. He received the tonsure from Mài Tǐrú and encountered an itinerant elder practitioner.

Seeing that the Master’s demeanor was extraordinary, [the monk] immediately presented him with the koan regarding the state before one's parents were born. The Master received this instruction reverently and practiced it in secret.
After investigating for many years, one day while on his way to a vegetarian feast, he suddenly encountered the braying of a donkey and attained great enlightenment.
Later, when the Elder Minshu passed through Mount Shih, the Master went to pay his respects and receive full ordination under him, and subsequently attended upon Master Tianhou.

[The Master] bestowed his seal of certification. Later, while residing at Wande Monastery, on the thirteenth day of the twelfth month in the tenth year of the Kangxi era (1683), at the hour of the Rabbit (5–7 a.m.), he gathered the assembly and finished his final instructions.
He then passed away while seated. His worldly age was fifty-two; his years of monastic seniority (*śrāmaṇera*) are not recorded. [The following is from] his discourse in the hall:
Lifting the head to see the sky, one sees through the face given by one’s mother; lowering the head to see the earth, one tramples over the pivotal point of ascent.
Even if you reach this state, you still lack the path for turning around. But what is this path for turning around?
After a long silence, he said, "Night travel is not permitted; you must arrive by first light. With a shout, he descended from his seat.
Zen Master Jiǔlóng Gǔyuán Jiàn of Dìngfén was a successor of Zen Master Tiānyìn Chóng. A native of the Yú clan from Chengdū, he took refuge in Qū during the chaos.
Jing ordained at Tongshan Temple and received the tonsure by the Canghai. He lived in seclusion on Mount Ji for several years.

Initially he visited Lingyin, and subsequently Lingyao, but neither accorded with him. He then visited Qushan, who accompanied him to the province of Chu; there he again visited Lingyin, yet still found no resonance.
He subsequently traveled to Jiangnan, where he visited Daxian at Jinling. He served as the Librarian (Zhizang) and later as the Rector (Weina).

Afterwards, he studied under Master Tianyin for formal certification. He resided at Longquan, Longbiao, and Huilong in Chu; he cleared the land to establish Cengshan; he returned to Qian to clear the site of Jiulong;
and he restored Tianlong Temple. Finally, he returned to Jiulong to pass away. His secular age was sixty-seven, and his monastic seniority...
Fifty. Ascending the hall, he brandished his whisk and said: "If one discusses this matter, it is not something proclaimed by the mouth, nor can it be fathomed by the mind.
It cannot be known through wisdom, nor can it be recognized through consciousness.

Even if you were to open a mouth as vast as space and wield a tongue as long as the rivers and seas, you would still be unable to utter a single word here—let alone to act with frivolity or recklessness; such things have already been met with laughter."
He kills those who merely look on. Entering the hall, he said: "The five thousand and forty-eight volumes of sutras are but old scraps of paper;
the three thousand seven hundred cases of kōan are nothing but rotten vines. Even if Linji and Deshan were to exchange blows and shouts, when they reach this point—"
It simply depends on having the capacity. Why? After a long silence, he said: "On three sides there is no need for armor; ten thousand miles away, songs celebrate the peace of the empire.
He ascended the hall and said: "An ancient said: 'There is one person who never eats food throughout their life, yet never says they are hungry.
There is another person who eats all day long, yet never says they are full. Now, tell me, you worthy ones: which one is it?"
"Right now, where is this person? If you say he is right before you, you cannot avoid mistaking a deer for a horse.
If you say he is not, that is like cutting off one's head to seek life. At this very moment, can you truly grasp him? 'The moon is clearly visible upon the tips of the plum branches.
Even seeing it at the tips of the branches is already late. [He lets out a shout and descends from his seat. *Upadesha* (Exhortation)
The Hall. Between the brows and beneath the forehead, the eyes are askance and the nose is straight. From the highest wisdom to the lowest folly, who is without their share?
Yet, when one arrives here, why is it that ten out of ten or five pairs cannot grasp it? Tell me, where does their fault lie?
He struck the whisk and said: "Precisely because it is so utterly clear, what is attained is made all the more delayed. He ascended the hall and said:
"I, this mountain monk, have a phrase that not even the thousand sages can do anything about.

I wish to reveal it to you all, yet I fear you will fail to recognize its good or bad, passing it by right before your eyes, needlessly stirring up turmoil instead of remaining at peace. Therefore, I do not dare to [speak of it] to you..."
[The Master] replied: "However, I have not yet examined whether any among you can directly and thoroughly comprehend this.

If you can so comprehend it, you will see that this mountain monk has neither affairs nor non-affairs. If you are as yet unable to do so, do not say that you have no doubts. He ascended the hall and said: "A bright pearl is held in the palm;
it distributes its luster according to the objects it encounters. A precious moon is suspended in the sky; it manifests its reflection when facing the water's edge. He struck the sounding block.
He strikes the meditation staff once and says: "Do you understand? The Elder Śākyamuni has descended into birth. Nine dragons spout water to bathe his golden body;
golden lotuses spring from the earth to support his two feet. Radiantly, from each of his eighty-four thousand pores, the Dharma-patience of non-arising is preached.
Solely revealed are his three hundred and sixty joints; from every joint, great jewel-light is emitted. Light upon light..."
It shines through and penetrates boundless worlds and lands as numerous as motes of dust.
Whether grass or wood, whether ordinary or holy, whether monastic or lay, whether male or female—indeed, including all that is sentient and insentient—all without exception behold its radiance.
Within that light, they obtain great benefit, great peace and happiness, great supernormal powers, and great enjoyment. Truly...
At such a time, is there anyone who is truly like this? There is. It is no hindrance to capture and defeat the Old Śākyamuni;
with the inexhaustible pure precepts of the three periods of time, one receives full ordination all at once without relying on words or phrases.

If there were none, the heavens would rain down the four flowers as auspicious omens, and the earth would shake in six ways to stir up dragons and clouds. [The Master] gave a shout and descended from his seat. He ascended the hall and said: "The mind of the Patriarch..."
Sealing the Iron Ox mechanism, he held it up for the assembly present to know: "It is not a phenomenon of seeing, hearing, arising, or ceasing;
do not casually seek it elsewhere. He ascended the hall and said: "Heaven does not speak, yet the four seasons proceed; Earth does not speak, yet the myriad things grow;
the Sage does not speak, yet the myriad states are at peace. But tell me, when a patch-robed monk does not speak, what then?"
The sun rises in the east at the hour of Mao; the conditions and causes are perfectly timely. The void is free from all obstruction; the great earth is brilliantly illuminated.
This matter is exceedingly clear—take care not to seek it elsewhere. Ascending the hall: The season is winter, and the cold is intense; the great earth is covered in vast, drifting snow.
The meaning of the Ancestor’s coming from the West is manifest and no different in two ways. If you understand it thus, [you have traveled] one hundred and eight thousand miles.

"Thousand! Do not understand it in this way; you would be failing those present before you. I dare ask you, all you practitioners of Zen: how, after all, must you investigate it so as not to fail those present?
Do you understand? *Pah!* When the snow melts, the clear stream flows; when the plum blossoms, the jade branches emit fragrance. Ascending the hall, he said:
"The heavens are cold and the earth frozen; water drips and ice forms. Śākyamuni the Old Man beheld the light in the night."
The stars; touching the nose, one loses the eyes. The grievance sinks into a sea of poison, implicating descendants for generations.

But tell me, what is it that implicates them? After a long silence, he said: "Fine rain wets the clothes, yet they cannot be seen; fallen flowers lie upon the ground, their sound unheard. Ascending the hall, he said:
"The north wind blows fiercely through the sparse fence; its piercing cold reaches the very bones, making one remember the beginning. Six years..."

The work was finished, yet he encountered the world mired in mud and fire; until this very day, who has truly known it? But tell me: where did the Old Śākyamuni encounter the world mired in mud and fire?

If you can understand this, you may well step forward to help rectify the collapsing纲 (gāng) [the fundamental order], thereby repaying the unrepayable debt of gratitude and employing the transformation of non-action (*wuwei*).
If this is not yet so, then even if your words penetrate beyond the limit of *Vaiśvānara* (the primordial ancestor), [you have not yet seen it].

The blue and yellow beneath the eyes are as far apart as heaven and earth. (He lets out a shout and descends from his seat. Small Assembly Sermon: If we discuss this matter, it is inherently possessed by every person;
it is not lacking in anyone. Yet, alas, throughout the twelve periods of the day, one’s karmic consciousness remains in a state of vast confusion, causing one to pass right by it face-to-face.
If you are one who truly roars like a bull elephant, you may rest assured that whether your eyes are open or closed, you will see clearly at all times.
For those whose heels touch the ground, let them go east or west as they please; naturally, at every step, they will tread upon it.
Thus it is said: "If you abandon it, you do not leave it; if you seek it, you err. Err, err! Even Buddhas and Patriarchs can never fathom its depths. Small Assembly.
He gave a shout and said: "The heavens are naturally high and the earth naturally thick; the sun and moon shine impartially upon the forests and hills.
How laughable, these men of substance—who do nothing but follow behind others. Even if their footprints cover the ends of the earth, in the end they remain as they were before.
He then offered this verse on the story of the Woman Emerging from Samādhi: "The night is cold and the frost is biting; the bright moon shines in the sky."
All come outside the curtain to play on the swing; as the night deepens, they buy wine, unaware of their intoxication. They are mistakenly led astray into a state of inverted suspension.
Zhaozhou visits the two hermits at the hermitage; when the boat reaches the riverbank, let it go as it will.
High and low, deep and shallow, waves of foam arise; hither and thither, the songs on both banks ring out swiftly. Leaves fill the sail with wind, and the sounds cannot be heard clearly.

Chanzhi Zongshi of Sishan Taiping was the son of the Xie family of Shu. He received the tonsure under me and, after long associating with Master Tianyin of Zhonghua, received full ordination and the seal of approval from him.
Upon taking up residence at the monastery, he ascended the hall and said: "The Yin reaches its extreme and the Yang returns;

the buds of a hundred plants open, bringing forth myriad realms. The Heaven revolves and the Earth turns; the blossoms of all fragrant flowers spread their splendor throughout the three thousand worlds."
This clarifies that there is no further matter remaining; heaven and earth share the same root, their substance being one.
When I, this mountain monk, announce it thus, it is much like casting turbid things into a pure vessel or scattering sand into the eyes of everyone present.

Is there anyone among you who cannot restrain your impatience? Come forth and exert yourself for the sake of the assembly! Look here! If there is none, I, this mountain monk, still have a second [turn].
"Two ladles of foul water have been splashed upon you all! [The Master] planted his staff upright, gave a shout, and descended from the seat.
Shi Qian Zhonghua Shi Zhu Hairen Chan Master was the son of the Zhang family from Kui Prefecture in Shu.
He went to Jingzhou to attend upon Master Tianhou, where he received the tonsure. He received full ordination under Master Mintu and remained in close attendance with Master Tianyin for a long time.
Together with [Master] Yin, he helped open up the Central Kingdom. He also traveled through Jiangnan, where his resolve to return home grew even firmer.
He served as *kuren* (supervisor) for over ten years, receiving certification from Master Yin. Upon taking leave, he returned to Zunyi in Shu to dwell in seclusion.
Later, when Master Yin passed away and the Central Kingdom remained vacant and desolate, the assembly urged the Master to succeed him on the seat.
Muitan Baeyun was the son of the Ge clan of Shu. His father, having fled the chaos, resided in Yelang; his mother was of the Peng clan.
She gave birth to him after dreaming of a monk begging for alms. At the age of twelve, he took refuge and received the tonsure under Yueo at Chaoyang Temple.
At twenty-five, he relied upon Tianfeng to receive full ordination. He studied extensively under Master Tianyin and received his seal of approval. The Master [Tianyin] said: "He shall not depart..."
This was his lifelong aspiration; therefore, he cleared this mountain to establish as his permanent residence.
Chan Master Beinan Chuanzhi of Duye was a dharma successor of Chan Master Tianhu Yin;
he was the son of the Mou family from Shu and had long studied under Master Tianhu Yin.

He was indeed so. By nature he was stubborn and arrogant; he once maintained the view that [the Buddha] would not appear in this world again. Throughout his life, he did not associate with those in power or high station.
He lived in seclusion at San Yuan An, halfway up Drum Tower Mountain in Yuncheng for over several decades, never crossing its threshold.

When the Prefect knocked on his door, he ultimately refused to offer him formal courtesy. When students sought his instruction, he remained silent. The monastics of all the mountains in the Yuncheng region held him in deep reverence.
He held the Way of the Teacher in high esteem. He constructed a stupa for his longevity on the slopes of Mount Wujiasi, ten *li* south of the city.

In the second month of winter in the *gengchen* year of the Kangxi reign, he addressed the assembly, saying: "On the sixth day of the following month, at the hour of the Dragon (*chén*), I intend to depart this world. The assembly took this to be a joke.
Seeing that the assembly did not believe him, on the fourth day he issued a notice to take leave of the various mountain monasteries. The various mountains...
The assembly gathered like clouds. The Master spoke again, saying, "How could a member of the monastic community consent to carry a corpse through the marketplace?

I wish to go out myself. At that time, the monks and laypeople of the entire prefecture responded with one accord; only the Prefect was skeptical and did not believe him. He issued a prohibition against the assembly, attempting to detain them by force.
Hearing this, the Master rebuked him, saying, "Foolish man! At such a time as this, let alone the Prefect—even if it were the Buddha himself..."
"Now that I have arrived, you cannot detain me either. Having finished speaking, he entered the shrine by himself and passed away while seated.
When the Prefect heard of this, he personally escorted him there immediately. At the time the pyre was lit, everyone smelled a wondrous fragrance pervading the fields.
After the cremation, the bone relics were collected and enshrined in a stupa. His worldly age was seventy-three, and his monastic seniority was fifty-six.
Chan Master Yanyue of Mount Feng at Anping Tiantai was the son of the Tu family of Anlong; his mother was surnamed Wang.
He received the tonsure at the local mountain under Master Youxuan and completed his full ordination under Master Yunfu. Yun assigned him the koan, "The myriad dharmas return to one.
The Master attended Master Yun while he resided at Puyang, Changshou, Yongning, and Zhonghe, remaining there for a long time. Later, he encountered Master Tianhu...

Shang arrived at the mountain. The Master insisted on keeping him there, and he frequently requested instruction. One day, while standing beneath the eaves, he suddenly became completely oblivious to his surroundings.
From noon until evening he regained consciousness; sweat flowed from his entire body, and he felt his mind and body were as light and agile as if he had laid down a burden of a hundred catties.
He then composed a verse and presented it to Hu, who immediately certified his realization and gave him instructions. He resided on this mountain for twenty years.
In his later years, he entered nirvana. His stupa was enshrined behind his home mountain. He was fifty-nine years of age and had forty-three years of monastic seniority (*śrāmaṇera*).
On New Year’s Day, he ascended the hall and said: "Yesterday was the thirtieth day of the twelfth month; today is the first day of the first month.

Cold crags and withered ravines have returned to spring; accumulated snow and frozen ice have been dissolved. The wooden man idly strokes his stringless lute; the stone woman plays her flute crosswise."
The Confucian flute. Now tell me, what about the Elder of Mount Tai? After a long silence, he inserts the incense and says: "The incense burns in the precious censer;
I pray for the Imperial House. He ascends the hall and says: "The World-Honored One transmitted the golden-brocade *kāṣāya* to Kāśyapa—when one moves the flowers, the butterflies arrive as well.
My Master bestowed the great red *pianshan* upon Xingyan—by buying the stone, one gains an abundance of clouds. If one is..."
"O eye of the monk! What need is there to open wide face-to-face? It is displayed clearly right before one's eyes. At Mount Kukkutapāda, it was a case of being left bewildered;
on Mount Dayu, they were mutually deceiving one another. Do you know this yet? If you do not yet know, then watch as I settle the case according to the facts.
[He strikes the meditation staff and descends from the seat. Entering the hall, he said: "The Buddha-body fills all phenomena..."
The realm universally manifests before all living beings; responding to conditions and meeting with those who call, there is nowhere it does not reach, yet it ever remains upon this seat of Bodhi.
Now tell me, what is this seat of Bodhi? He then drew a circle with his whisk and said:
"At this point, out of ten people there are five pairs. Unless one is deceived face-to-face, one will surely pass it by right at the head. Right now—"
"Is there anyone who has not missed it? For now, call him here to wash the old monk’s feet. The Mid-Autumn Small Sermon:
"The Buddha-dharma of all quarters fills the mountains and seas; only at Tiantai is there not a single character.

Today, as this auspicious Mid-Autumn festival arrives, I ascend the hall and sit in silence—*zhuilu-du*. After a long while, he drew a circle (○) with his whisk and said: 'Fortunately, there is still one.'"
This is not so; otherwise, you would be failing this very moment.
I wonder from where this has come? Looking left and right, he said: "Do not seek it in the heavens; do not look for it in the water. Small Assembly (Xiaocan):
Ignorance and the nature of consciousness are themselves Buddha-nature; the illusory and empty body is itself the Dharma-body. With his whisk, he drew a circle and said: "This..."
"This one is ignorance; which one is Buddha-nature? Again, he drew a circle and said, "This one is Buddha-nature; which one is ignorance?
Again, he drew a circle and said, "This one is the illusory body; which one is the Dharma-body? Again, he drew a circle and said, "This one is the Dharma-body;
which one is the illusory body? "O assembly of monks, I, this mountain monk," [acted] like...
This is an analysis. How do you all understand it? If you can understand it, you may call it ignorance, yet you may also not call it ignorance;
you may call it Buddha-nature, yet you may also not call it Buddha-nature;
you may call it the illusory body, yet you may also not call it the illusory body; you may call it the Dharma-body.
One might say it is not called the Dharma-body; thus, it is so, yet it is also not so.
Although this is the case, I myself would have to receive thirty blows of the staff for saying such a thing. Why? Have you not heard it said:
"He who comes to speak of right and wrong is himself a person of right and wrong"? Question: "What is the place where all Buddhas emerge? The Master replied: "The plum blossom."
[Flowers] bloom amidst the snow. [A monk] asked, "What is the家风 (house style) of the Jibei lineage? The Master said, "Drops of blood on the tip of the staff.
[A monk] asked, "It is not within, it is not without, and it is not in between. Where does it reside? The Master struck him and said, "Look, then, where it is!
[A monk] asked, "What is the heart-essence of the ancient Buddhas? The Master said, "Stonehead. The monk pressed further.
"What is the Supreme Vehicle Dharma? The Master said, "A fence. The student asked, "I do not understand. The Master said, "To keep out cattle and to keep out horses.
(This concludes the section on) Chan Master Tianyu Huai, a successor of [the aforementioned master].
Xian'an Yunjingshang was a native of the Liu clan from the local district; because his father held an official post in Lin’an, Yunnan, the Master accompanied him there.
On a day of leisure, he visited Mount Ji (Ji Shan) and visited Shengfeng Temple with a sense of joy. Suddenly, he resolved to renounce the world and become a monk.
His father sent people to persuade him, but he did not return. He subsequently went to the local temple to receive the tonsure under Venerable Heya and requested full ordination.

Later, he cleared a patch of ground at Shizi Lin (Lion Grove) and lived in seclusion for several years. Because he felt that the Great Matter remained unclarified, he resolved to travel as a wandering monk.
He arrived at Bainu Sandgang in Zunyi, Sichuan, where he met Venerable Tianyu; there, he attained realization and received certification.
Having returned to his native village, he established the Yunjiao Monastery and opened the Dharma for over twenty years, never stepping beyond its threshold.

In the final month of autumn in the year Ding-si, one day, manifesting a slight ailment, he informed the assembly and passed away. His stupa was enshrined at the foot of the mountain; he was seventy-three years of age.
At forty-eight years of monastic seniority (*saṃgha-lakṣa*), he ascended the hall. "Sūtra, Vinaya, and Abhidharma; precepts, concentration, and wisdom.
Reaching forward to grasp his head, then turning back to grasp his back: "A frog in the fire swallows the moon; though one looks at it from every angle, it is still not understood.

Even if you were to understand, you would still be like a blind donkey following the great herd. He gave a shout and descended from the seat. He addressed the assembly: "I originally have a secret formula for seeing..."
He spoke thus for the sake of the assembly, intending to ask further how [it was].
As the monk reached out with his staff to strike him on the head, the Master said, "The Elder’s bright pearl—where is it?
Just as the monk was about to open his mouth, the Master struck him. Often, there were none who could grasp his pivotal point.
Chan Master Guiping Ding of Guiyu in Yongxing, Guizhou, was the son of a mother from Tōngchuān in Shǔ.

He received the tonsure at Zhōnghé Temple in his native region and entered Qián to seek certification under Upādhyāya Tiānyǔ. He resided at Wànshòu, later moved to Dōngshān, and finally passed away at Yongxing.
Entering the hall for a discourse, he said: "The skull constantly interacts with the world; the nostrils touch upon the family style. [He] employed...
Thus, he vies in wealth with the Eight Great Dragon Kings; yet when not employed, even half a coin is not worth its weight.
Arriving at this point, it would be enough to churn the long river into cream and curd, and transform the great earth into gold. But tell me: where does the power lie?
After a long silence, he raised his fly-whisk and said: "The golden arrowhead, well-tuned, has already fought a hundred battles;
the iron whip, full of strength, regrets having no enemy. With a shout, he descended from the seat. Ascending the hall, he said: "Wanshou opens the mouth of the sack;
the lofty nostrils and golden fur run forth. One day they fill the earth as qilins; each one faces south to gaze at the Big Dipper. Regarding these four lines:
Within this there is a single phrase that can grant freedom and can seize, can kill and can bring to life.
If one can investigate and penetrate it, the task of study throughout a lifetime will be completed; furthermore, one will act with the same hands and eyes as the thousand sages.

Can you do so? He strikes the meditation staff and says: "Moving the boat, one understands the currents; raising the oars, one distinguishes the waves. He addresses the assembly: "The spring wind thaws the ice."
When the sprouts of the hundred grasses emerge, there is a single phrase; if you look upon it, your eyes will go blind. If you can realize this, I grant that you possess the eye of study.
Chanshi Hui of Guihuan, Changshou Puyang, was a son of the Chen family from Changyi in Shu-dong. Due to the changes of the times, he entered [the monastic life].

Chan Master Anlong Yüquan Xianjinda Gu, whose secular surname was Li, was a native of Xi’an. He received the tonsure under Fáyún at Yútàixū Dōng and received full ordination under Nánhuá.

Chan Master Guiyang Xiachang Haiwei was the son of the Liu family from Sinnan. He received the tonsure under Venerable Dongshan Meixi.
