Gather it all and leave it to him as he wills. His mind enters the gate of emptiness while his body remains at home; he sheds his court robes to don the *kāṣāya*. In Bodhi there is no duality, for originally there is no tree;

when the ground of the mind is cool and clear, one turns the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. If the six sense-faculties suffer affliction, do not harbor doubt elsewhere—the illness of the mind must be cured by the medicine of the mind.
Facing the wall for nine years without a single word, he leaves people with nothing but this: a sense of being struck by something extraordinary.
He marveled at this rare occurrence. Master Yuan asked, "When Niutou had not yet met the Fourth Patriarch, why did the hundred birds bring flowers and the devas present offerings?
He replied, "When the flowers bloom, bees and butterflies gather. Yuan asked, "After he saw [the Patriarch], why do they no longer come?"
The scholar said: "The fruit ripens while the tree-top remains empty.

The Layman San-yi, surnamed Long and named Yuansu, was the son of [the aforementioned]. In his youth, because of his intense longing for the Way, he gave his entire household to support monks and Daoists.
One day, he encountered Songkui, who questioned him: "The old woman east of the city was born at the same time as the Buddha."
For what reason did he wish not to see the Buddha for his entire life? The gentleman wrote these words: "He is a man, and I am a man.

The Layman of the Six Perfections was the son of the Li family of ancient Diany; his mother was the Lady You. At fifteen, while watching a performance of the *Xiangshan* (Fragrant Mountain) drama, he conceived the thought of renouncing the world.
His parents would not permit it, but fortunately the elder master Xiachang exhorted him, saying: "In the past, there was the Great Being Vimalakīrti..."
He acts as a teacher for humans and devas, discoursing on the Dharma-gate of non-duality; yet, is he not also a lay bodhisattva?
You should follow my words, and later you will naturally find their benefit for yourself. The scholar Zunxia followed these instructions as if they were the commands of his parents.

There was a Confucian scholar named Huang Zhongcui, who was directed to visit Master Shanhou, through whom he attained the point of entry. Later, he visited Master Shanguan to receive certification of his realization.
The *Ji* (Collection) has a table of contents, recording only three instances of circumstantial dialogue (*jīyuán*), one verse, and the following exchange:
A monk asked, "It is not mind, it is not Buddha, and it is not an object. What is it? The Master [Zhaozhou] extended both hands and said, "What is it?
The monk said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "Do not blame me. Another monk asked, "The entire great earth is a single fiery pit."
"Why can you not leap out? The Master said, "The entire earth is a single pit of fire. As the monk hesitated, the Master said, "You are burned to death!
One day, as the Master walked with his staff held upright, a monk pointed at it and asked, "What do you want to do with this?"

The scholar said, "On the slippery road, one completely relies on the power of others. He spoke in verse: "Only by putting on clothes can one avoid the cold; By eating food, one puts an end to hunger.
As for the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West— What is it but the back of a worn-out donkey?"
Chan Master Gusue Zhi of Dongshan in Qianxi was a dharma successor of Chan Master Baxia Shansong Muzong, the fifth generation of Tiantong and the thirty-fifth generation of Linji.
A native of eastern Sichuan, he studied under and received certification from Venerable Muzong.
Ascending the hall: Today is the fifth day of the fifth month, the Dragon Boat Festival. At this thatched gate, no mugwort tiger is hung. How could the season be allowed to pass in vain?
Taking up the five poisons, we boil them together; Mingzhou’s Cloth Bag has eaten his fill, and he has devoured Chizhou’s Luzu.
What a great song—do not be reckless! A sweet melon is sweet to the very stem; a bitter gourd is bitter from root to tip. Ascending the hall: On the first day of the New Year...

The spring has returned to the six realms; in every house the gongs resound, and in every household the drums are beaten. The great leap with joy, while the small dance. Only Dongshan is different from the world:
he is accustomed to wielding his single-bladed white staff with reckless abandon.

Tossing it about and brandishing it upside down for years on end, he beats the Buddhas and the Patriarchs day after day. Suddenly, there is one who comes forward, unable to bear it from the sidelines, and says: "This..."
"Old man, you do not understand the ways of the world; you know only yourself and are unaware of others. The mountain monk then struck him with his voice and sent him away. Why was this so?
"Let the blue seas change as they may, I shall never communicate with you. Relying on his staff, he descended from the seat. Entering the hall for the discourse:
"The east wind has blown for days, causing the myriad sprouts to emerge; the peach and plum blossoms have fully bloomed before the mountains. Roll up [the screen]..."
The person coming through the curtain is seen by all; to whom does this one phrase before the throne belong? Speak quickly! Speak quickly! Small Assembly.
The drum beats and we enter the hall. This is a ready-made case. The candles shine and the incense rises.

If you do not realize it thus, yet if you do realize it, then the realms of infinite lands are not separated from a single hair-tip; ten ages of past and present do not depart from the present moment.
"If you do not offer [an answer], let me see how I, this old monk, shall judge you for you. He dragged down his staff, descended from the seat, and struck everyone present into dispersal.
Chan Master Ciyun Canglong Yu, a successor of Chan Master Songmei Hai, was the son of the Zhang family of Lu'an in Jiangnan. He resided to the west of Qian.
At Mount Shan, he paid his respects to the Elder Gaosong, received the tonsure, and attained full ordination. He studied under Master Gaosong Mei and received formal certification (*inka*).
He resided at Ciyun and passed away there; his stupa was enshrined at the mountain’s base. His secular age was seventy, and his monastic seniority (*sengla*) was forty.

Ascending the hall, he said: "Prajñā is like the great sun-disk: when it rises, heaven and earth are universally illumined. It is like a great mass of fire: when one approaches it, it burns away one's face."
The Gate: Like a drum smeared with poison; when struck, all who hear it perish. When lifted up, heaven revolves and earth turns;

when set down, the seas are calm and the rivers clear. But as for neither lifting nor setting down—everyone carries the pearl from the Red Water, and every individual embraces the jade from Mount Jing.
Now, regarding this single phrase of the household shrine being secure and sealed: how do you speak of it? After a long silence, he said:
From this point on, one does not return; once returned, one attains it. Who can vie for the misty scenery of the Five Lakes?

Ascending the hall, he said: "Heaven has no four walls; the earth is cut off from the eight directions. A single expanse of clear sky penetrates through past and present. It is luminously free from coming and going; it is distinctively without front or back. Therefore it is said:
'The numinous light shines alone, utterly transcending the sense organs and their objects. Its essence reveals true permanence, unconstrained by anything.'"
"Words and letters. The nature of the mind is unstained; it is fundamentally and spontaneously perfected. Simply by being free from delusive conditions, one is the Buddha of Suchness (*tathatā*).
To call it 'Suchness' is already a transformation. But what is the message of that which does not change? After a long silence, he said, "In the morning I ate thin rice gruel;
in the afternoon I felt hungry again. He gave a shout and descended from his seat. He ascended the hall [again] and said: "Before the Buddha appeared..."
In this world, every person’s nostrils point toward heaven, and each one’s heels touch the ground.
Since the Buddha appeared in the world, everyone’s eyes have had sand added to them, and each one’s ears have been filled with water.

Among these, if there should be even one or half a person who has nothing to grasp above and cuts off all self-identity below, coming forth to say that ordinary people and sages are no different and that past and present are of one consistency—it would not be an obstacle.
"What joy! What fulfillment for my entire life! If it were not so, I, this mountain monk, would further add dust and grime upon it.
He struck his staff and descended from the seat. Ascending the hall, he said: "Bright as the sun; black as lacquer. The true does not conceal the false; the crooked does not hide the straight.
For six years on the Snowy Mountains, he endured hunger in vain; for nine years at Shaoshi, he sat facing the wall in folly. If, within this, one possesses the eye that discerns the Dharma..."
"I simply lie down on dry ground beside the sheep; how could I be willing to stand in his snowy fields? Although this is so, "Without the spring breeze, the flowers will not bloom;
for the flowers to bloom, one must borrow the power of the spring breeze. With a shout, he descends from his seat.
Chan Master Chang Lingyou of Wei Yang Huayan was the son of the Hu family in Jingzhou. Encountering a period of social turmoil, he joined the military and entered Qian.
At the age of twenty-seven, he earnestly yearned for transcendence from the mundane world; he took up residence at Jiulong Mountain and took refuge with Master Yanju.

Furthermore, he personally visited Master Sōng at Xishan. Later, he paid his respects to Sōng and received the tonsure and full ordination; he requested instruction from both masters, who clarified the teachings for him, and he received their formal certification (*inka*).
He subsequently established the Dharma of the *Lotus Sūtra* and the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, and later moved to Wo-yun. Afterward, he traveled to Chu province. Ascending the hall, he said:

"The spiritual mechanism operates in secret, and the precious sword is fully revealed. Cutting through a thousand differences, true permanence is uniquely exposed. In every instance, the wondrous is manifest. Objects...

The radiance of all things shines forth; a single path of pure emptiness penetrates through past and present. Brightly manifest, it transcends coming and going; clearly distinct, it is free from all opposition.
It sits firmly atop the crown of Vairocana, yet does not uphold the teachings of Śākyamuni. Reaching this point, what need is there to speak of "taking charge wherever one is"?

Meeting conditions is itself the fundamental principle. Directly, one attains the cessation of ten thousand functions; even the thousand sages cannot carry it away. Furthermore, regarding this transcendent single phrase—how do you speak it?

[He] gave a shout and descended from his seat. Ascending the hall, he said: "The mirror of wisdom is perfectly bright; the myriad dharmas are all empty. The light of prajñā is uniquely revealed; delusion is exhausted and reality is complete.
In every dust mote and every land, majestic authority is universally manifested. In every object and every instance, it is entirely [present]."
To manifest wondrous function is to have the dragon roar and mist rise, the tiger sigh and wind arise;

even tiles, pebbles, and stones all leap about, while mountains, rivers, grasses, and trees resound and shake the earth. This is the most supreme among the supreme, the most extraordinary among the extraordinary.
But tell me, what is the single phrase for responding to conditions in daily life? (He brandishes his whisk and says: "Scoop up water and the moon is in your hand; play with it..."
The fragrance of flowers filled his robes. He ascended the hall and, holding up a *bāzāo* (plantain tree) to the assembly, said:
"If you have a staff, I give you a staff—this is 'placing a head atop a head. If you have no staff, I take away your staff—this is 'seeking life by hacking off the head.
Old Bāzāo, his resources exhausted and his strength spent, has nowhere to open his mouth; he acts upon the tip of the staff."
As for livelihood, it is not so here with this mountain monk. If there is something, I do not give it; if there is nothing, I do not take it away.
I simply cause him to cast off his entire being, leaving not even a single thread of attachment. Pure and naked, bare and clear—this is the news of arriving home.
Where else could there be a single thing to act as a condition or an object of opposition for people? Do you understand? Not seeing a single thing...
The Dharma is the Tathāgata; this is what is called Avalokiteśvara. A brief informal discourse (*xiaocan*). An ancient worthy once said: "If you seek the ox, you must follow its tracks;
in studying the Way, study the mindless state. When the tracks are found, the ox returns; when the mind is absent, the Way is easily realized.
Right now, if someone among the assembly were to come forward and say, "The tracks are right here; where is the ox? you should answer him directly.
The Way: On the banks of green willows and fragrant grasses, there is nowhere that does not honor it. Then another man comes forth and says, "I am originally without mind;
where, then, does the Way reside? He replies to him, "Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, it is always present within."
Furthermore, there was one man who came forward and said, "A man of spirit has his own will to soar through the heavens; he does not travel where others have trodden.
When the old monk heard this, he could do nothing but swallow his breath and stifle his voice. Why? Because a single grain of rat droppings can defile an entire pot of soup.
The evening *can* (general assembly) of the Lantern Festival: Before the fifteenth day, the mud ox at the bottom of the sea contains the moon.
"Go! After the fifteenth day, the stone tiger before the cliff will cradle its child and sleep. On the very fifteenth day, the stone man will hold his board and strike it amidst the clouds;
the wooden woman will clasp her sheng flute and blow it from the bottom of the well. When presented to the lantern, it will laugh until its mouth splits open.
This groundless, sudden occurrence is a scene of error. He struck the ground once with his staff and said: "The mountain monk’s staff is as alive as a dragon. One.
He has already swallowed it whole. Thirty years hence, one will avoid the need to knock over bricks and smash tiles.
Chan Master Huang Juci of Shiquan was the son of the Liang family from Tongchuan in Shu.
He entered Qian at Fenghuangchi on West Mountain, where he received the tonsure under Venerable Yushong. Having received the seal of approval from [Master] Mei, he resided at Jiulong.
Ascending the hall upon leaving the monastery: I dwelt at Longshan for three or five years; once the debt of the plow and harrow was settled, I withdrew my body.
With straw sandals and staff like dragons and tigers, I ask: how many fellow travelers are there? The old man Xuefeng shouldered his *zhili* staff and walked on without looking back;
the Great Being Maitreya stands waiting at the crossroads. But tell me, what of the Elder of Longshan? Furthermore—
"How do you establish this? He struck the meditation staff and said, "Three steps outside the gate, there is a different style of wind.
He ascended the hall and said, "The ancients said: 'The lush green bamboo is entirely True Suchness; the dense yellow flowers are nothing other than Prajñā.'"

Today, Huangshan has switched the head for the tail and turned the ancient into the present. Taking this *tathatā-prajñā* (suchness-wisdom), he has transformed it into a vast monastery (*mahāvihāra*).
He intends to ensure that the dragons and elephants of the ten directions, upon reaching here, each dwell within it in the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*).
At this very moment, if one calls it a vast monastery, it is again *tathatā-prajñā*; if one calls it...
“True Suchness Prajñā is also a vast monastery. How can one attain its true measure? He struck his staff once and said:

“The halls and pavilions atop the mountain peaks are a legacy of a thousand ages; the triple gate stands high, facing the great site of flourishing activity. He then ascended the hall for the formal discourse.
The large month has thirty days; the small month begins on the first. Upon reaching this point, for the time being, not even a thousand sages can know it, nor can the Buddhas recognize it.
Do you all recognize it? If you do, I will grant that you may enjoy its use while on the road.
If you do not, the Nine Dragons will not begrudge their compassion; they will act according to their nature to provide each of you with a way home.
What is the news of the ultimate? What is the news of arriving home? After a long silence, he threw down his staff and said, "This too is like a turtle poking its head through a broken wall.
This was the teaching style of Chan Master Ding, a successor in the lineage.
Chan Master Xinghui Zhen of West Mountain in Guiyang was the son of the Ge family of Xi'an.

He paid homage to Master Zongfeng, received the tonsure and full ordination, and was both certified and sealed by him. Regarding his verse on Huating Chuanzi: "A wild mind is still superior when by the river's edge;
With a short oar and a long song, he steers the iron boat. Had it not been for Jia Shan coming to change his hands, He would have only taught how to row across."
In what year of the donkey? Huanglong’s Three Barriers: "What is my hand like the Buddha’s hand?"—beat to death the mud-pig and the scabby dog;
strip away the sweat-soaked undershirt until it is gone. At will, pluck the flower and break the willow. "What is my foot like the donkey’s foot?"—trample through Zhaozhou’s drawbridge.
Striding freely and alone across the great square, let the monks speculate as they please. Every person has [it].
A man’s place of affinity: an old fisherman with a belt-tethered boat sleeps the night deep within the reeds; at dawn, he scratches his head and gazes at the heavens.
Regarding the Chan Master Wumie Huiying of West Mountain, who received the seal of mind from Master Zongfeng, [the latter] cited the words of Dongshan Shui: "The water..."
The Verse of Shangxing says: "The place where all Buddhas are born: On the water, the mountain flows eastward. Clouds part and the red sun emerges;
Rain falls and green moss grows."
Master Yunfeng Zugu (Cloud Peak Zu Gao) of Zhifei Hermitage at San Chao Water, a Dharma successor of Master Poshijing, was the son of the Fu family of Shu.

Due to the chaos of war, he entered Qian, where he stayed at Mount Mouni in Guiyang. There, he paid respects to Yuekong and received the tonsure, and subsequently relied upon the elder Yushong for full ordination.

He was fully ordained under Master Poushi, from whom he received the Dharma. He resided at Zhifei for several decades. In the second month of autumn in the Wuchen year of the Kangxi era, he announced to the assembly that he would pass away and entered parinirvāṇa.
His stupa was erected to the south of Ben’an. He was seventy-seven years of age and had forty-six years of monastic seniority.

Ascending the hall, he said: "The Great Way is fundamentally right before one's eyes. What need is there to say that it is difficult to behold? [He strikes the meditation seat once with his staff and says:
If you behold it, everyone should realize Yunmen’s 'Universal. If you do not behold it, you are from Xiqin and I am from Donglu.
He gave a shout and descended from the seat. On the Buddha’s Birthday, he addressed the assembly: "Pointing to heaven and pointing to earth was already a labor in vain. Seven...

Pacing around in circumambulation, one only invites further calamity. This provokes Yunmen to exercise his true command; thus, for generation after generation of his descendants, the illness remains most severe.
Regarding Chan Master Xingzheng, a successor of the Dharma lineage of Chan Master Xianqi:
he was the son of the Wu family of Fuzhou, Jiangxi, but was born while residing in Sichuan. While there...

At Huayan Cave in Anshun Prefecture, Qian Province, he received the tonsure before Master Lide. He traveled to Danshan to study under Master Yusheng, and later studied under Master Minshu to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*).
Subsequently, he returned to Danshan and remained in seclusion for three years, receiving the seal of his mind from Master Yusheng.
At the invitation of Hou Yansheng, the Military Commissioner, he ascended the hall; [he said: "Tree after tree, the green pines..."
Firm in his later years, each stalk of green bamboo resounds with the pure wind; extending his life for a thousand ages, the lamp’s brilliance shines forth.
The springtime beyond the kalpas is utterly unlike this one. But what is the message of that which is not like it? After a long silence, he let out a shout and descended from his seat.
At Wanshou Monastery in Zhuding, he ascended the hall and said: "Yesterday I sat within the Hall of the Ancient Buddhas;
this morning at Wanshou I reveal the karmic conditions. Carrying my staff, I seek only those who understand me; everywhere the green mountains display their smiling faces.

But tell me, what is the matter therein? He looked to his left and right and said: "In the morning one watches white clouds stretching across the ridges; at night one observes the bright moon shining."
Before the steps stood Master Zhao Tianzong of Yulongjing Temple in Guiyang, a native of the Wang family of this province. His mother was of the Chen clan.

At Lianhua in Guizhou, he received the tonsure from Master Zishan and received full ordination under Master Miyun. He practiced both the esoteric and exoteric paths; subsequently, while reading the Chan [scriptures]...
Guān Cè advanced and saw that Huangbo was addressing the assembly, saying: "A monk asked Zhaozhou, 'Does a dog have Buddha-nature?
Zhaozhou said, 'No. Simply, throughout the twenty-four hours of the day and night—while walking, standing, sitting, or lying down;
while dressing, eating, defecating, or urinating—keep your attention focused on this single word 'No. With intense alertness, maintain it at every moment."
The word "Mu" (無). As days and years passed, it became fused into a single whole. Suddenly, the flower of the mind blossomed, and he awakened to the pivotal mechanism of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
Thus, he was no longer deceived by the tongues of the elder monks throughout the land. An immediate state of doubt arose within him;

yet, for the time being, having nowhere to seek instruction, he could only burn incense in the stillness of night and take a vow. He took up the "Mu" koan for himself and began his investigation during the day.

At the night assembly, he forgot both body and mind entirely. After practicing in this manner for a long time, one day while he was walking in meditation (caṅkrama), he suddenly heard the cry of a crow and attained the point of entry.
He resolved to travel extensively to seek instruction from various masters.

While traveling through Yunnan, he encountered Master Yusheng, who asked him, "What is the matter of your pilgrimage? The Master replied, "A fool runs about outside. Yusheng said, "Why have you come here?"
The Master said, "Traveling together along the mountain path, each person looks at the wind and mist before their own eyes. Nanquan said, "I only fear those who feign clarity.
The Master said, "Even you, Reverend, must not treat the noble as the base. Nanquan deeply approved of this.
After the Master received the Dharma, he established the Yulong Monastery, named Hongfa Temple. He ascended the hall and said: "The Great Way has no form; the Ultimate Truth has no name."

Manifesting transformations according to the directions and shifting the scales of expedient means, a spiritually sharp fellow seizes a fragment of this and immediately understands how to spread a net that covers the heavens, disperse a forest of thorns, churn the long river into cream and curd, and transform the great earth into gold.
Seated within a mote of dust, he turns the Great Dharma Wheel, suddenly causing all sentient beings to see alike, to be enlightened alike, to attain alike, and to realize alike. [The] patched robe...

The monks were at the height of their spirits; they were like dragons gaining water or tigers relying on a mountain. Yet, though it was thus, this was still merely a matter on the periphery of the gate of transformation.

If one discusses the single path that transcends this, even the Buddhas of the three periods find their mouths hanging upon the wall, and the patriarchs of successive generations can only suppress their breath and swallow their voices.
Consider, for instance, Huangbo’s three severe blows of the staff upon Linji—tell me, was this the upward path?
"Is this the ultimate path? Is this a matter on the periphery of the gate of transformation? After a long silence, he said: "The embroidered mandarin ducks emerge from the golden needle;
yet you further take that golden needle and pass it to others. With a shout, he descended from his seat.
Chan Master Dàqiān Zōngyuè of Zhèníng was a native of Bǎi in Guǎng'ān, Shū Province.

A monk asked, "When an ox passes through a window frame, its head, horns, and all four hooves have already passed through; why is it that the tail cannot pass? The Master struck him and said, "You fastidious lacquer bucket!
The monk stepped forward and said, "In that case, it must shake its head and wag its tail. The Master said, "Do not be so careful."
Avoid being too close to others. Addressing the assembly: Beyond the limit of Vīradhvaja, there is no more confusion;
to take it up directly is already to have missed it. Cherish the very point of the original source: when the wind blows through the stone mortar, it chants "Mahā.
Small-scale instruction: What thing comes in such a manner? It cannot be formed into a ball, nor can it be split apart. Treading upon a scale-weight, one realizes it is originally iron.
The heavens are high and the clouds are clear; the moon has just begun its return. Let us set aside for a moment the moon’s return. But as for what the ancients said:
"Cultivation and realization are not non-existent; defilement is simply not permitted. How do you all deliberate upon this? (He strikes the meditation staff once.)
The title of *Zhuangyuan* (Metropolitan Graduate) is originally ordained by Heaven; do not mistake Feng Jing for Ma Liang.

This is the biography of Chan Master Chang Huijing Yongfeng Xianan, a successor of Chan Master Yu Xian Ying, whose family name was Wang and who hailed from this local prefecture. His mother was surnamed Wu. He received the precepts in the city...
He had long heard of the tonsure and dyeing robes [of the master]. He visited Master Xian of Shishan to receive his seal of approval. The Master then established Yongfeng as his place for retirement.
A monk asked, "What is the Buddha? The Master said, "I am a man from Pucheng. The monk said, "What is the meaning of the Patriarchs' intent?
The Master said, "When climbing a mountain, one breathes with shortness. The monk said, "By what means is this cured? The Master said, "Sit, sit."
Once again:
Qingzhen Puxing Huiji Yun Chan Master was the son of the Liu family of his native district.
He received the tonsure under Master Wenzhi of this very temple and completed his full ordination under the elder Qiling Chisong. He subsequently sought certification from Master Shishan Yuxian.

He again resolved to travel as a wandering monk. While traveling through the region of Chu with Lianzhou, he once composed this verse: "Holding precepts and practicing Chan— To be bound by no ropes, yet bound oneself.
It is not like that at all; Vivid and distinct, clear and open. If anyone asks about the meaning of the Patriarch, I tell them:
'Place your hat upon your head. Ha ha!"
Chan Master Jiu-long Yue-heng Zhen-sheng of Ding-feng was a dharma heir of Chan Master Gu-yuan Jian.
Born into the Zhang family of Guiyang, he received the tonsure at the age of ten under Master Bing-xue at Yuan-tong Temple in his native region.
He first studied under Master Hui-lin, but their karmic affinity did not harmonize; subsequently, he went to study under Gu-yuan.
Jian Faming personally received his seal of certification. After Yuan passed away, the assembly urged the Master to succeed him on the seat, but he did not consent;
he subsequently closed the gate within his Woyun (Clouds Resting) chamber.
*Qian-Nan Hui Deng Lu*, Scroll Seven;
*Qian-Nan Hui Deng Lu*, Scroll Eight.
Compiled by Ruchun of Tianlong, Xian’an.
Chan Master Sheng of Anping Tiantai was a successor of Chan Master Yuefeng Yan.
A native of the Zhou clan from Sichuan, he was born in Anshun Prefecture, Qian Province, at Qiandang Chaoyin Temple, where he received the tonsure under the master Ziran.
He subsequently went to study with Yuefeng Huo at his own mountain monastery.
Shang approved [of this]. After Feng passed away, the assembly urged the Master to succeed him on the seat. He remained in seclusion at Yinyi Hall for three years.
Upon leaving his retreat, he resided constantly on this mountain. He ascended the hall and said: "Breaking through the profound barrier, I release the iron hawk;
it pierces the void into two sides. The stone maiden before the cliff nods her head and laughs. But tell me, what is she laughing at? She laughs!"

This mountain monk falls from his own head and falls from his own feet. (He lets out a shout and descends from the seat. Ascending the hall, he says: "Precepts are the foundation; conduct is the wall.
Guard against light and heavy transgressions with vigilance. Old Man Poshan speaks thus, knowing only that opening one's mouth is easy, yet failing to realize how long one’s tongue has grown.
Haining, however, is not like this: "Precepts are the foundation; conduct is the wall. When cold..."
Facing the fire for warmth and seeking coolness by riding the breeze—it is not that these people give rise to arrogance; it is entirely because this matter is beyond all deliberation.
Is there anyone here who can transcend deliberation? If so, you should come forth, overturn the meditation seat, and shout the assembly into dispersal!
"At this very moment, not only is the old man Poshan defeated, but he also gains a great sense of liberation. Is there anyone who can do so?
If not, I, this mountain monk, shall directly employ skillful means. He then recited the precepts and descended from his seat.
Ascending the hall, he struck the meditation staff and said: "Buddha to Buddha, it is this that is transmitted; patriarch to patriarch, it is this that is passed on.
The old monks of the world, past and present, explain it horizontally and vertically—it is this they explain.
The patch-robed practitioners of the ten directions and the oceans, investigating horizontally and vertically, investigate this. Now tell me, what is this? After a long silence, he said: 'Cutter.'"
Do not harbor conjectures. Entering the hall, [the Master said]: "This matter originally has no handle; yet each and every thing has its own provenance.

When walking along the road, one takes steps while admiring the moon; when raising one's eyes, heaven and earth are entirely within the range of vision. Why need one ascend a high tower? Mountains are vast and flowing, waters are vast and flowing;
the expansive, penetrating, and perfect luminosity is gathered within a single mirror. With a shout, he descended from his seat. Entering the hall, he struck the sounding block.
The staff-bearer said: "The infinite Dharma-gates and hundreds of thousands of wondrous meanings are all here, ground into a hundredfold mess.
Yet you still instruct Upādhyāya Ning to wag his three-inch tongue, beat his two pieces of skin, prattle of yellow and white, and point east while drawing west;
in the end, he will never do it. Why is that? When people are level, they do not speak; when water is level, it does not flow."
Chan Master Xuanjing Guangjing of Yunjiao Xianan was a dharma heir of Chan Master Dingxiang. He was the son of the Tao family of his native region.

In his youth, his parents sent him to this mountain monastery, where he paid respects to his preceptor, Chan Master Dingxiang, to receive the tonsure and the full precepts. He followed Master Ding for more than thirty years.

Before he had even left the seat of his master, Zhiying inscribed the lineage and the instructions of entrustment upon his head. However, because the Master [Xuanjue] was determined to remain in obscurity, he firmly declined the succession.
After Zhiying passed away, the Master inherited his robes and bowl and succeeded him on this mountain.

Chan Master Jin’an Pujing of Yingshan Monastery in Zhenyuan was a dharma successor of Chan Master Guizong of Mount Heng. A native of the Song family from Ping’le in Yuexi, he resided at Fenghuang in Shiqian, where he received the tonsure under Mount Heng.
He then received full ordination under Yunche at Xilin Hall in Shibing, after which he further studied under [various masters].
Certified by Master Hengyue. He resided at Yongxiang in Shibing and extensively renovated the Yingshan Monastery, dedicating himself particularly to receiving guests;
his later life is not recorded.
[This concludes the record for] Chan Master Zhuhuaiyin, the Dharma heir of [Master].
Master Xianfeng Sheng of Xishi was the son of the Cheng family of this prefecture. His mother was of the Chen clan.
He received the tonsure from Master Mingxin at City Yuantong Temple and vowed to travel as a wandering monk. He followed Master Zhuhuai of Yuzhen Mountain together with his own teacher.
While traveling through Yunnan, he arrived at Wuhua Temple and received full ordination from the elder Ban-sheng.

The elder assigned him the koan, "The myriad dharmas return to one," whereupon [the Master] simultaneously overturned the lacquer bucket. Later, when the elder certified his realization, he remarked, "This son shall succeed you.
Following the elder’s command, [the Master] could not bear to part with his teacher; thus, the teacher assisted him in returning to Qian, where they resided.
For more than ten years at Yuzhen, he exerted all his strength to lead the assembly, never shrinking from toil or sweat, until he finally received formal authorization (*kṣānti*).

Later, departing from Huai, he passed through Wucun and extensively reclaimed Shixia as a place for his final years. His disciples had previously constructed a stupa for the Master at the foot of the mountain.
He ascended the hall and said: "The Xafeng Peak is small, yet surrounded by many mountains; winding waters meander about it, clearly [illuminated]."

The hall is perfectly suited; there is no need for the slightest contrivance. It is simply established by the earth and fashioned by heaven. Arriving here, one values only that the person and the environment are in harmony;
naturally, everything becomes the ultimate Way (*tīdao*). But what is the ultimate Way? After a long silence, he said:
"If it were not for the early blossoming of flowers along the purple road, how could one see the yellow oriole alight upon the willow branches? He struck his staff and descended from the seat.
Ascending the hall, he said: "The hands grasp and the feet run; the eyes behold forms and the ears hear sounds.
Only the tongue desires to speak, and it no longer discriminates between the distant and the intimate. Since it speaks, why does it not discriminate between the distant and the intimate?
He struck the meditation staff once and said: "A distant relative is not as good as a neighbor. Ascending the hall, he struck the meditation staff.
One person said, "The sky is clear and the sun is shining. Another person at the table said, "It is raining and the ground is damp.
Yet another person at the table asked, "Do you all know where Xishan’s staff lands when he acts for others?
For forty-nine years, the Old Śākyamuni chattered away; when did he ever speak to this point? Although I, this mountain monk, today possess but a single..."
With a compassionate heart, examine this: even giving money to create such a situation is committing a sin. Now tell me, what kind of sin is it?
Then, striking the table once, he said: "I have no excuse."
Xian An-yu Zhenxuan Yiru was the son of the Sun family of this province.

At the age of thirteen, while at Zongchi Hermitage, he received the tonsure from his preceptor Zhu Huai and was simultaneously granted full ordination and formal authorization (*kṣānti*). Later, he resided at his home mountain until the end of his life;
his stupa was erected at its foot. He lived to the age of forty-nine.
Chan Master An Shun Jingming Meiji Zong was a dharma successor of Chan Master Zu Bi Zui.
He was the son of the Cai family from Ruining in Henan. At the age of nine, during a period of social upheaval, he fled to the South of the Ranges.
There, he suddenly contracted a malarial fever, which prompted in him the aspiration to leave the mundane world. Once his illness had subsided, he took refuge in Xue... [text continues]

The master Yanjing requested instruction on the *nienfo* (Buddha-recitation) kōan. Later, upon encountering the "Tongue-Sound" [kōan], he was directed to visit the elder Yuedang at Shibao Mountain in Duan.
There, he received the tonsure from Benshi and subsequently received full ordination under Yuedang. He then studied under the patriarch Bi and received his seal of approval.
Ascending the hall, [the Master said: "To seek upward or downward is like digging the earth to find the sky; to seek the Buddha or seek the mind is like washing soil in mud.
How can this compare to right here, where one simultaneously cuts off the heads of all Reward-Buddhas and Transformation-Buddhas? It is like the bottom of a bucket falling away;
only then is one called a person who has finished their business. As for Elder Zong, you usually sit upright and sleep horizontally atop a solitary peak. Today, you have been..."
Driven by others, one cannot avoid being caught within the multitude. Disregarding danger and ruin, he briefly reveals a single thread to his fellow brothers.
He then beckons the assembly with his whisk and says: "Tell me, is this single thread the mind? Is it the Buddha? After a long silence, he says:
"The embroidered mandarin ducks are displayed for you to behold; I do not hand the golden needle over to anyone. He then pulls his staff and descends from the seat.
The Seat. A verse on the saying "The myriad dharmas return to the One. Where does the One return? The void shatters.
Only the stone man is permitted to listen with his ears pricked. Responding to things according to capacity, he rolls freely along. At the break of dawn, the red sun shines upon the fresh mountains.

Chan Master Guizhou Guanyin Pujie Dachuan, a successor of Chan Master Shanguan Weiquan, was the son of the Chen family of Annam. Having verified his mind under the guidance of Master Shanguan of Songkui, he ascended the hall and said:
"Beating the drum in the midst of the Cloud of Compassion Mountains, I ascend the hall within the Guanyin Hermitage. He leaned upon his staff.
The staff-bearer leaps up and lands upon a heap of refuse, bumping into the King of Vows of Samantabhadra at Mount Wutai.
He utters some "householder’s Zen"—a jumble of fragments—that prevents the learned Ānanda from coming to the council.
This deceives Kumārajīva, who was translating the scriptures into the language of Tang; he reports back, "Luo lu li li po luo."
The Master ascended the hall. Deshan entered the gate and immediately struck him—a public reward for one and a secret punishment for another.
Linji met people and immediately shouted—a spring decree being enforced in winter. Those who transcend the ordinary do not fall into traps; how could those with the true eye be deceived?

Therefore, the pivotal mechanism of the ultimate path is a single source for all sages; the message within this is no different from that of all Buddhas. It is like a flash of lightning striking a flint.
Fire! How can one afford to blink? If you are a true hero, you will know as soon as you are pressed; why wait to enter the water or the mud?
If you are dull-witted or stagnant, the hawk has already flown past to Silla. Do you understand? To manifest the ancient path through every movement is not to fall into the trap of silent stillness.
Small Assembly. This is the家风 (house style) of Linji and the essential secret of Deshan: one blow, one scar. One...
Holding a handful of blood in his palm, responding to each capacity as it arises, he uses one wedge to drive out another. With a grandmotherly heart, he is direct and cutting for the sake of others.
How many know gratitude and understand how to repay it? Do not say that we are merely indulging in empty chatter. Small-scale discourse: I, this mountain monk, have a secret method;
it is the most intimate way to enter the Way. Do not seek it through sound or form; do not attempt to fathom it with the intellect or the mind. If you intend to ask further—
"How is it? With this, the staff struck him on the head.
Puan Songkui Tianyi Daoyue was the son of Lü of Chunan. During the chaos, he entered Qian, where he stayed at Longtan Temple in Annam.
There he paid his respects to Master Wuxia and received the tonsure. He then went to study under Master Shanquan at Songkui. One day, while at Songkui...

While serving as an attendant to the Chancellor, he engaged in a discussion on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* with an official. When they reached the passage where the World-Honored One raised his hand and questioned Ānanda, the Master suddenly attained a state of awakening.
He immediately informed the Chancellor, who then confirmed his realization. After the Chancellor passed away, the Master succeeded him as the abbot of this mountain for over ten years.
One day, manifesting a slight illness, he addressed the assembly and settled his final affairs; he then sat in the lotus posture and passed away. His stupa was enshrined at the temple.
At Old Tashan in the west, his worldly age was sixty-seven and his monastic seniority forty years.

Ascending the hall, he held up his staff and said, "Opening the gate of the patriarchs and unfolding the家风 (family style) of the ancient Buddhas. He struck the ground once with the staff and said, "Clearing the true path for humans and devas."
He sweeps away heterodox schools. Again, he strikes the ground once and says: "The Treasury of the True Dharma Eye is now circulating at once.
Do you all know where the staff of Songgui acts for others? To those who take it up here, I strike three thousand blows in the morning and eight hundred in the evening;
to those who stick out their tongues behind my back, I likewise give thirty blows. Not yet finished.
"He must surely be willing to grant you entry. Why is that? [He] strikes the desk once more and says: "In the heavens, all stars bow toward the North; among men, no water flows but toward the East.
He then cites the case of Baoshou opening the hall: when Sansheng pushed forward a monk, Baoshou struck him.
Sansheng said, "If you act as a teacher in this manner, you will blind the eyes of the entire city of Zhenzhou! Baoshou then threw down his staff.
He returned to the abbot’s quarters. The Master said, "The two great elders employ such tactics;
one might think they are acting according to the mandate, yet alas, the bystanders laugh. Under the gate of Songgui, it would be best to bury them all in a single pit.
But tell me, where does their fault lie? Let those with eyes try to judge. He ascended the hall and said, "Deshan’s staff was like a rain of points; Linji..."
A shout like a thunderclap—how different from the heroes of a chaotic age!

Śākyamuni’s silence in Mahādevī’s chamber and Vimalakīrti’s sealed mouth in Vaiśālī are exactly like spies in a time of peace; they must be relegated to the lower wind before one can reveal the nostrils of the Ultimate.
But what are the nostrils of the Ultimate? After a long pause, he said: "Even if you were to realize it right here..."

It is clear. This too is a case of making a special occasion of it. Entering the hall, [the Master said]: "The rice of Luling and the radishes of Zhuzhou—this mountain monk has always enjoyed them with ease.
Today, I have specially brought them forward for all of you. Do you understand? If you can understand..."
"Let us grant, for a moment, that you may enjoy [the Dharma] along the way. But if you still do not understand—let alone three forming a flock or four making a troop—consider this:
even as this mountain monk admits his own defeat, do you all know where the point lies? After a long silence, he said: "Three lifetimes, sixty kalpas. Tsk!
Ascending the hall, he struck his staff once and said: "The Buddhas of the three periods of time are also like this."
It is so. The ancestral masters of successive generations were thus; the old monks of the world were thus.
When Elder Yue arrives here, he cannot but be thus. But tell me, what is this "thus"? Again, he struck the ground once and said: "Kai! (or "Strike!")
"I see that the Lamp-Light Buddha’s original radiance and auspicious signs were like this. [He] ascends the hall and says: "Zen, Zen, Zen!
Whether speaking or remaining silent, whether moving or still, the essence is ever serene. Dao, Dao, Dao! Eating, drinking, dressing—who lacks anything?
Since it is thus, for what reason did the youth Sudhana travel through one hundred and ten cities and rivers, visiting fifty-three spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*)?
After that, he saw Mañjuśrī again; only then did he attain realization. But tell me, what is it like after realization? "The flowers bloom in the Upper Garden, yet it is not spring;
the sun rises from Fusang, yet it is not early. Entering the hall, [the Master said]: "As for the Buddha-dharma at the beginning of the new year:
Jingqing says 'it exists,' and he too deserves thirty blows. Mingjiao says 'it does not exist,' and he too deserves thirty blows. Why is this?"

What "existence" or "non-existence" has anything to do with the Buddha-dharma? Even if one were to say, "It is neither existent nor non-existent," one should still strike them across the back with a staff.
Why is this so? [He] strikes the staff once and says: "The staff opens its seal; when practicing benevolence, do not yield."
A Verse on the Story of Beholding the Morning Star: Beholding the morning star, the field of vision broadens; throughout the great trichiliocosm, there is nowhere for shame to lodge.
Clearly, the clouds have dispersed and the moon shines in every house; in vain did he endure the six years of cold in the deep mountains.
All phenomena return to the One; all phenomena return to the One—where does that One return? An old fisherman hooks the misty waves upon the river; the reeds on both banks secretly open their eyes.
The water-fowling mandarin ducks flew far away to avoid him.
Chan Master Guangfu Xue'e Dazhao of Annan was the son of the Chen family from Jiangling in Chu.
While at Shibaoshan in Yiliang, Yunnan, he received the tonsure and ordination under Venerable Yuechang, and subsequently relied upon Master Songkui of Puan in Qian.
Quan received full ordination and certification. He resided at Guangfu Temple. A monk asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
The Master held up a fruit dish and said, "A handful of walnuts. The monk asked, "How many are there in a handful of walnuts? The Master said: [He held them out.]
"Three before, three after, three times three. The monk said, "Three before, three after, three times three. And how many is that? The Master said, "You have immeasurable transgressions;
I too have immeasurable transgressions. The monk said, "But as the saying goes, once a gentleman’s word has been spoken, even four horses can hardly overtake it.
The Master then struck him, saying, "Out of pity for a three-foot child, I have lost my two rows of eyebrows."
The Master passed away at Guangfu; his stupa was erected beside the temple.
Chan Master Wanshou Shen-shi Benzhao of Annam was the son of the Yi clan from Western Sichuan.

Having lost both parents in his youth, he resolved to leave the household life and received the tonsure from a monk named Yixing at a small hermitage in his native region. Vowing to travel as a wandering mendicant, he eventually reached Qianzhou.
Pu’an went to Mount Songkui to pay respects to Master Shànquán and requested the full precepts (*upasampadā*).

Shànquán held him in high esteem and once led him in investigating the koan of the dog having no Buddha-nature. One day, while carrying firewood out of the work area, the yoke of his wood-laden pole slipped;
at that moment, he suddenly attained realization and wrote this verse: "How extraordinary! How extraordinary! The brush has slipped away; both ends are gone, yet it remains in the middle."
"From beginningless kalpas until this very day, you have failed to recognize this present moment and have repeatedly suffered defeat.

He presented this to Baiquan, who said, "Under the clear blue sky and bright sun, why do you pretend to see gods and ghosts? The Master said, "From this day forward, I shall no longer allow you, Old Monk, to deceive me.
Baiquan said, "Even if you recognize this present moment, it matters not; there will still be 'another time' and 'a later day.'"
The matter remains. The Master said, "What will happen at some future time? Before the words had even ceased, Quan struck him with a flurry of blows.

The following day, he wrote out the lineage transmission and handed it over as his final entrustment. The Master resided at Wanshou Monastery in Annan, where he opened the Dharma for the reception of disciples for over twenty years;
from beginning to end, his practice remained consistent. On the first day of the first month of winter in the year of Yi-chou, he passed away and was interred in a stupa outside the West Gate.
At the foot of Mount Qinglong, he ascended the hall and said: "When not a single thought arises, all conditions suddenly cease. The constant radiance appears before you, solitary and vividly clear.
What more need be said of matters beyond [the ordinary] or the extraordinary pivot? Even if one were to examine this, it would still be like sucking the broth from within a steamed bun.
Do you understand? Put on clothes to avoid the cold; eat food to stave off hunger. If you attempt to ask 'How is it?'—*bang*!"
"Breaking the donkey's spine. One day, while the Master was at a meal in the home of a lay donor in the city, a gentleman asked, "Among the three teachings, which one is the most honored?
The Master said, "If you ask, then none of them are honored. The gentleman said, "According to what the Old Monk says, there is no distinction among them at all.
The Master said, "That does not mean they are all indistinctly the same. The gentleman said, "In that case, ultimately..."
"Which teaching is the most honored? The Master said, "When the elephant roars, the earth trembles.
The monk said, "If the Old Monk acts like this, you are merely playing a trick. The Master said, "If one plays tricks, one falls into hell as fast as an arrow.
He asked a monk, "Where have you come from? The monk said, "I have come from Anlong. The Master said, "I heard that Mount Dapien was stolen by someone; is this true? The monk— [remained silent].
The monk said, "How can you, Preceptor, deceive me right to my face? The Master said, "Tell me the truth. The monk was speechless.
The Master said, "A fellow with a dragon's head and a snake's tail! Begone! A monk asked, "What is the Yunmen cake? The Master said, "Half a catty, one whole.
The monk said, "I am not asking about this cake. The Master said, "I expect you will be unable to consume it."
Chan Master Puan Biyun Hengxian Shengmu was the son of the Xiong family from Jiangyou. While residing in Annan in Qian, he followed his father to Duxiu Mountain where he received the tonsure.
There, he studied under Master Shanquan to seal his mind. He ascended the hall and said:
“Śākyamuni before, Maitreya after—needlessly, each makes false discriminations. The Zen of the Tathāgata, the secret instruction of the patriarchs—how laughable!”
Everyone is deluded by this. Biyun makes such a critique; tell me, where does his intention lie? He strikes the staff once and says:
"Of all the waters on earth, none do not flow east; among the stars in heaven, all point north.
With a shout, he descends from the seat. Ascending the hall, he says: "Yunmen’s 'dry shit-stick,' Dongshan’s 'three pounds of flax'—casually and suddenly brought forth."
"I have suspected many people of being killed. Is there anyone among you who is not suspected? Come forward and try to say something!
As soon as a monk stepped out, the Master struck him and said, "I was walking through the wild weeds, and you have already fallen into a deep pit. He then drove him straight down from the seat.
Ascending the hall, he raised his staff and said: "The Buddhas of the three periods have never exhausted its use; the patriarchs of successive generations have never exhausted its use;
the old monks of the world, past and present, have never exhausted its use. Today, it has fallen into the hands of Biyun."
"Tell me, how is it? [He] strikes the gavel once and says: 'Able to exercise the true command. Ascending the hall, he said:
"Lifting up your eyes, you do not see the sky; lowering your head, you do not see the earth. As for these three-footed mortals of the human world, they all say it is not so.
Even if you could say it is so, this staff would still not grant its approval. *Duḥ!*" Ascending the hall, he said: "The Great Luminous Treasury is eight-sided."

Linglong. It encompasses and harmonizes the ten voids, penetrating through both antiquity and the present. Heaven and earth rely upon it for their covering and supporting; the sun and moon rely upon it for their illumination and descent.
Sages rely upon it for their governance and transformation; the Buddhas rely upon it to transmit the mind.

He sought certification from Venerable Shanquan and subsequently resolved to travel extensively. Returning home from Zhejiang, he resided at Mount Tianlong, later moved to Songkui, and again resided there.

Chan Master Jichang of Xudeng in Duye was a successor of Chan Master Shengkewu.
He was the son of the Wang family of Puyi in Hubei. His mother was surnamed Chen. Because the region was in turmoil, he entered Qianzhou at his birth.
At the age of thirteen, upon hearing his mother recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, he conceived a desire to transcend the mundane world and followed Master Ben’an.
Juchechuan, having severed his worldly attachments, received full ordination from Master Meixi of Dongshan in Guizhou. He subsequently sought certification under Master Shengke of Huayan in Sichuan.
Addressing the assembly, he said: "The true void is fundamentally serene; from where could illusory obscurations arise? Buddhas and patriarchs employ empty names;
their teachings for saving sentient beings are likewise but words of delusion. If you are a person of transcendent capacity, there is no need to raise this up again and again. One.
The West River dries up in his mouth; with a single blow, he forgets where he is staying. Shaking out his sleeves, he departs from Chang’an—how can he deceive this staff?
But tell me: what excellence does this staff possess? Seeing his cheek behind his head, it does not engage in coming and going.
Chan Master Wuxia (Venerable Elder) of Dūyún was the son of the Xu family of this prefecture. He left home at Kaihuà Temple and took Cānshí as his teacher.

He received full ordination under Venerable Tiānyě Guǎngēn. The Master was skilled in maintaining his integrity; for several decades, he never engaged in the business of acting as a matchmaker for others.
He remained composed in his austere simplicity until the end of his life, when he sat upright in his seat to instruct the assembly before passing away while seated.
His worldly age was fifty-one, and his monastic seniority (śrāmaṇera-vassa) was thirty-six.
Chan Master Zhuya Xing of Luping in Pingyue, a successor of Chan Master Bilingmen, was the son of the Zhu family from Duan County in eastern Sichuan; he left the household life [to become a monk].

At Anshun Yuan Tong Temple, he received the tonsure from Hengming and, relying on the Elder Yushong, received full ordination. He studied under Master Bilin and received his certification of realization.
On the Buddha’s Birthday, he ascended the hall and said: "Pointing to heaven, pointing to earth, he alone claims supremacy;
this matter belongs only to those of extraordinary capacity. Gautama has fully revealed his profound intent—how many can recognize this kindness and know how to repay it? Thus it was said.
"Now, is there anyone here who knows how to repay kindness? "There is. "The staff of Cimeng will beat him until he is broken; I have not yet let go of it. Why?
Because in the school of patch-robed monks, rewards and punishments are clear and distinct. The Master, at the time of his death, spoke a verse to the assembly and passed away while seated.
His stupa was erected on the southern slope of his native mountain. His worldly lifespan was sixty-three years; his monastic seniority exceeded forty years.
